title: Acintyabhedābheda
description: The Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava doctrine of acintyabhedābheda (inconceivable simultaneous oneness and difference), associated with Jīva Gosvāmī, stating that the relationship between Kṛṣṇa and his potencies is beyond logical categorization.

title: Advaita Adhyāsa
description: In Advaita Vedānta, adhyāsa (superimposition) is the erroneous attribution of the qualities of the non-self (anatman) to the self (ātman).

title: Advaita Ajāti-vāda
description: The Advaita doctrine of ajāti-vāda (non-origination), associated with Gauḍapāda, asserting that the world of birth and death never truly originates and that Brahman alone is real.

title: Advaita Avidyā
description: In Advaita Vedānta, avidyā (nescience) is the beginningless ignorance that veils Brahman and projects the world of multiplicity.

title: Āgamic Tradition
description: The Āgamic (Tantric) tradition: the Śaiva Āgamas (28 principal texts), Vaiṣṇava Pāñcarātras and Vaikhānasas, Śākta Tantras; their structure (jñāna, yoga, kriyā, caryā), their role in temple ritual, iconography, and initiation (dīkṣā).

title: Alaṅkāra Śāstra
description: Alaṅkāra-śāstra is the theory of poetic ornamentation, systematized in the work of Bhāma Kṣapa (Bhāma) and culminating in the treatises of Uṃāśambhu (Kāvyas, 10th c.) and the later tradition of Jñāna Kṣapa (12th c.). It enumerates the thirty-one figures of speech (alaṅkāras) such as alliteration (anuprāsa), simile (upamā), exclamation (utprekṣā), and the ten poetic defects (doṣas) and thirty-eight merits (guṇas, e.g. śleṣa) that render a composition aesthetically effective (rasa). The śāstra distinguishes primary (bādhāra) and figurative (gīya) ornaments and prescribes their deployment to evoke the eight rasas (ṣāḍhārane) defined in the Nāṭyaśāstra (cf. rasa-theory).

title: Anubandha Catuṣṭaya
description: The Anubandha-catuṣṭaya ('the four-fold adjunct') is the traditional opening inquiry of a Vedānta work posed by Śaṅkara's bhāṣyas: adhikārin (who is fit to hear), viṣaya (what is taught — Ātman-Brahman), prayojana (why — mokṣa), and sambandha (the relationship of teacher-text-and-student). These four conditions ensure that jñāna-yoga rests on a qualified hearer, a valid scripture (śruti), a competent teacher (guru), and a clear purpose (mocana). The framework recurs in the Brahma-sūtras (the 'prasthāna' of reason) and the Gītā's gradual method.

title: Āpaddharma
description: The Dharmaśāstra concept of āpaddharma (dharma in times of distress/emergency): the relaxation of normal rules for survival, the hierarchy of permissible actions, and the principle that normal dharma resumes when the emergency passes.

title: Apparatus Criticus
description: The critical apparatus is the scholarly apparatus of a critical edition recording variant readings, editorial emendations, and source-witness identification for each lemma. Its forms include the positive apparatus (listing witnesses supporting the chosen reading), the negative (listing rejected variants), and the hybrid. Modern standards (CSE, Leuven, Cambridge conventions) encode sigla (e.g. * for corrections, † for deletions) and witness sigla; digital critical editions (CEEC, Muktabodha, Sarit) render apparatus relationally (TEI <app>) so that a reader may traverse the editorial argument and reinstate alternatives.

title: Arjuna
description: Arjuna (अर्जुन) is the third of the Pāṇḍava brothers, a Mahāratha archer and the interlocutor of the Bhagavad Gītā. The Mahābhārata (Vana, Vāra, Karṇa, and other Parvas) recounts his deeds: the burning of the Khandava forest with Kṛṣṇa, his conquests, and his role as the charioteer addressed by the Gītā's teaching. He is father of Abhimanyu by Subhadrā, and his descendants receive the succession of Hastinākṣa. As a character he embodies the warrior's dilemma of duty (dharma) versus kin, resolved under Kṛṣṇa's instruction.

title: Artha
description: Artha (अर्थ) is material prosperity, power, and worldly security, the second of the four Puruṣārthas and the practical ground of social order. In the Dharmaśāstras artha is to be gained by righteous means (dharma-saṃmukha), pursued through the householder stage (gṛhastha āśrama) as the engine of society and the support of the sacred (yajña, dāna). Kautilya's Arthaśāstra treats artha as the science of polity and wealth, but subordinated to dharma. The Gītā subordinates artha to dharma: dharmārtha as the first consideration of action, while affirming the legitimacy of worldly engagement for the karmayogī.

title: Āśrama Dharma
description: The four āśramas (stages of life) in Dharmaśāstra: brahmacarya (student), gṛhastha (householder), vānaprastha (forest-dweller), and saṃnyāsa (renunciant).

title: Āśrama
description: Āśrama (आश्रम) refers to the traditional four-stage scheme of Hindu life: brahmacarya (student), gṛhastha (householder), vānaprastha (retired), and saṃnyāsa (renunciate), the social and spiritual framework of the varṇāśrama-dharma system. The Gītā (6.1–2) treats saṃnyāsa as the crown of the āśrama sequence; the Dharmaśāstras (Manu Smṛti 3–6) elaborate duties (dharmas) of each stage, particularly the householder's support of the sacred (yajña, bhakti, dāna). The āśrama system was historically a means of integrating spiritual aspiration with social duty and is variously reinterpreted in modern reform movements (Rammohan Roy, Swami Vivekananda).

title: Atharvaveda Śākhās
description: The recensions (śākhās) of the Atharvaveda: Śaunaka (the principal surviving recension) and Paippalāda (partially preserved in Kashmir and Orissa).

title: Ātman
description: Ātman (आत्मन्) is the innermost self or principle of individuation, the subject-of-experience for whom the Vedic ritual, the Upaniṣadic investigation, and the Yoga path are undertaken. The Upaniṣadic dictum 'tat tvam asi' (Thou art That) sets ātman against the supreme reality, Brahman, and raises the question of identity versus difference answered variously across schools: non-dualistically in Advaita (ātman is Brahman), qualified non-dually in Vaiṣṇṇava and other traditions, and dualistically in Sāṃkhya/Yoga and the Āstika Darśanas. The Gītā describes mokṣa as realization of the imperishable ātman, 'not the destructible body.'

title: Bhagavad Gītā Chapters
description: The Bhagavad Gītā is structured in 18 adhyāyas (chapters), traditionally arranged by topic: the first chapter (Arjauna-viṣāda) presents the battlefield grief; chapters 2–6 cover the yoga of knowledge, action, and meditation (karma-, jñāna-, dhyāna-yoga); chapters 7–12 describe the higher knowledge of the Supreme (para-parigraha) and the yoga of devotion (bhakti-yoga); chapters 13–18 culminate in the instruction on the field (kurukṣetra) covering the field-and-knowing-field (kṣetra-kṣetjñā-viveka), renunciation, and the threefold faith.

title: Bhagavad Gītā Philosophy
description: The philosophical teachings of the Bhagavad Gītā: the synthesis of karma-yoga (selfless action), jñāna-yoga (knowledge), and bhakti-yoga (devotion); the nature of the self (ātman), the supreme (puruṣottama), the three guṇas, and the concept of svadharma.

title: Bhakti Movement
description: The Bhakti movement (7th–17th centuries): the devotional renaissance across India emphasizing personal devotion (bhakti) to a chosen deity (iṣṭa-devatā) over ritual orthodoxy; its poet-saints (Āḻvārs, Nāyanārs, Vārkarīs, Haridāsas, Rāmānanda, Kabīr, Tulsīdās, Mīrābāī, Sūrdās, Caitanya).

title: Bhakti
description: Bhakti (भक्ति) is devotion — love, surrender, and reverence toward a personal deity (īśvara) or guru — and is the central practice of the Vaiṣṇṇava, Śākta, and Śaiva devotional traditions. Originating in the early-tamil Āḻvār/Nayanmar poetry (c. 6th c. BCE–5th c. CE) and the Brahmanical epics, bhakti was systematized by Rāmānuja (śaraṇadhīna) and particularly by Chaitanya Mahāprabhu (mahā-bhāgavatānvīta). The Gītā (12) addresses the bhakta who fixes the mind on the supreme person. Bhakti is cultivated through hearing (śravaṇa), chanting (kīrtana), worship (puja), and surrender (praṇāma/prapa), distinguishing it from jñāna- and karma-mārga.

title: Bharatanatyam Repertoire
description: The traditional Bharatanatyam performance repertoire (mārgam): alarippu (invocation), jatisvaram (pure dance), śabdam (lyric dance), varṇam (centerpiece), padam (abhinaya), tillāṇa (finale), and ślokam/maṅgalam (conclusion).

title: Bhedābheda Avibhāga-bheda
description: The Bhedābheda doctrine of avibhāga-bheda (difference-in-non-difference), asserting that the whole and its parts are simultaneously different and non-different (like fire and its sparks).

title: Bhedābheda
description: Bhedābheda ('difference and non-difference') holds that the individual self (jīva) and the supreme (Brahman/Īśvara) are simultaneously distinct and non-distinct depending on the epistemic standpoint. Classical sources are the Udgīta of the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad, the Vedānta-siddhānta, the Viśiṣṭādvaita of Rāmānuja and the Dvaita-influenced Vedānta of Nimbārka and Vallabha, and the Gauḍīya school of Jīva Gosvāmī, who grounds bhedābheda in the Rāsa-līlā. It opposes both Advaita's identity and Dvaita's difference, articulating relationality (saṃbandha) as a substantive structure of reality.

title: Bhīṣma
description: Bhīṣma (भीष्म) the 'terrible one', grandson of Śāntanu and the Ganga, is the grandsire of the Kuru dynasty, famed for his lifelong oath (vrata) of service to the throne on the bed of arrows (śāpa-bodha). The Mahābhārata places him in command of the Kuru army against the Pāṇḍavas; his discourse on statecraft (rājādharma), the law of war, and the fourfold dharma is recorded in the Śānti and Anuśāsana Parvas. He dies on the bed of arrows (by Karṇa's arrow) and is the archetypal kṣatriya who subordinates personal happiness to the lineage (vansha).

title: Brahman
description: Brahman (ब्रह्मन्) is the supreme reality or ultimate ground of being in the Vedānta tradition, described through two complementary registers: neti neti (not this, not this) negation in the Bāṣkala Upaniṣad and affirmative definition (sat-caitā-tāṇḍya-vijñāna) in the Taittirīya. Brahman is the material, efficient, and final cause in different schools: the impersonal Brahman of Śaṅkara, the personal Brahman of Rāmānuja and Madhva, and the bhakti-oriented Brahman of the Gauḍīya tradition. It is the substratum of cognition (sat), consciousness (caitanya), and bliss (ānanda), the source and goal of all beings.

title: Carnatic Rāga System
description: The Carnatic rāga system: the 72 melakartā (parent) rāgas organized in the kaṭapayādi formula, their janya (derived) rāgas.

title: Camakam
description: The Camakam, the second part of the Śrī Rudram (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.7), listing the desired boons for the yajamāna.

title: Chandas
description: Chandas (prosody) is the Vedāṅga governing the quantitative and accentual metre of Vedic and classical Sanskrit verse. It classifies metres by gaṇa (syllable-groups) and vṛttas (lines of equal length), the fundamental schemes being the Gayātri (24 syllables, 8+8+8), Anuṣṭubh (4×8), and the jāti metres of the Ṛg Veda. The canonical text is Pingala's Chandaḥśāstra; the discipline also comprises the three-syllable weight analysis (laghu, guru, pūrṇa) and the rules of yamaka, anuprāsa, and other figures of speech (alaṅkāra-vāda). Mastery of chandas is prerequisite for correct Vedic recitation and the aesthetics of classical kāvya.

title: Codicology
description: Codicology is the study of manuscripts as physical artefacts: support (palm leaf, paper, birch bark), layout (margins, pradéli text-blocks), scribal practices (colophon, correction, addition), quire structure (chapters, catchwords), and binding. Descriptive standards (CDLI, MMS, Digital Index of Middle-Eastern Manuscripts) capture material, paleographic, and provenance data. For Sanskrit, the palm-leaf (talapatra/birch) format, the vertical orientation, and the use of yellow or red inks mark regional traditions; the discipline grounds textual criticism by distinguishing scribal from authorial variation.

title: Collation
description: Collation is the systematic comparison of manuscript (or print) witnesses to identify and record their agreements and disagreements, the first stage of establishing a critical text. Manual collation (by eye, against a copy-text), mechanical collation (19th-c. comparators), and digital collation (CollateX, Juxta, e-Annotated) produce variant matrices. The result feeds the critical apparatus: witnesses are grouped into text-types (recensions) and weighted by age, provenance, and fidelity to the archetype, enabling stemmatic or eclectic reconstruction of the most probable original reading.

title: Colophon
description: The colophon (nāmadheya) is the scribe's termination of a manuscript, typically recording the scribe (likhita), date (saṃvatsara), place (desha), patron (dattarāja), and invocation of merit (puṇya). Colophons reveal transmission history: they name regional scripts (e.g. Grantha, Devanāgarī, Malayalam), date works to specific reigns or festivals, and expose corrections, multiple scribes, and ownership chains (pustakapratāpti). In printed editions colophons record the editor's source and corrections; for critically-edited Sanskrit texts the colophon is a datum for the apparatus and provenance.

title: Critical Edition
description: The scholarly reconstruction of a text from multiple manuscript witnesses, applying textual criticism to establish the most probable original reading.

title: Dāna Types
description: The classification of dāna (gift) in Dharmaśāstra: nitya (daily), naimittika (occasional), kāmya (desire-motivated), and vimukti (liberation-oriented).

title: Dāna
description: Dāna (दान) is the practice of charitable giving, a key householder duty (karma) and one of the principal means (puruṣārtha) of social merit. The Dharmaśāstras (Manu 4.138, Yājñavalkya 1.258) distinguish the four kinds of gift (amṛta-dāna, dhānya-dāna, jñāna-dāna, and dāna to Brāhmanas), and the Gītā (17.20) grades giving by the giver's motive (sattva, rajas, tamas). The gift (dāna) is the 'eye of the giver' in Buddhist and Jain ethics and a central śrāddha (ancestor) practice.

title: Darśana
description: Darśana (auspicious sight): the act of beholding a deity, guru, or sacred object in Hindu practice; its theological significance as a two-way exchange of grace (the deity sees the devotee, the devotee sees the deity).

title: Dharma
description: Dharma (धर्म) is a core Sanskritic concept whose meanings range from duty, law, and righteousness to the intrinsic nature or essence of a thing. In the Vedas dharma is coeval with cosmic order (Ṛta); in the Dharmaśāstras it becomes the regulatory norm governing duty by āśrama and varṇa; in the Buddhist teachings it denotes the teachings and the constituents of experience. The term is context-sensitive: svadharma (one's own duty) in the Gītā, mānuṣadharma (human duty), and sanātana dharma (eternal order) represent later Indian-religious usage. Dharma operates in dynamic tension with artha, kāma, and mokṣa (the four puruṣārthas), and its specification is a central concern across the Darśanas.

title: Dharmasūtra
description: The Dharma-sūtra (the 'thread/sutra of dharma') is the earliest genre of Dharma literature, composed in the terse sutra style and attached to each Vedic school (Apastamba, Gautama, and Vāśiṣṭha of the Yajur; the Āpastamba of the Ṛg). It treats the law (dharma) — the duties of varṇas and āśramas, the life-cycle rites (saṃskāra), and the 'means' (upāya) — in the 'three worlds' (triloka). It is the direct antecedent of the metrical Smṛtis (Manu) and the fountain of the Dharmaśāstra tradition.

title: Digital Humanities
description: Digital humanities applies computational methods to humanities inquiry: corpus text-analysis (tokenization, POS, parsing), network analysis (knowledge graphs), image processing (HTR/OCR for non-Latin scripts), and digital critical editions. In Indic studies the field supports the digitization of Sanskrit corpora, the markup of critical editions in TEI so that variant witnesses and editorial interventions can be queried relationally, and the mapping of textual, geographic, and temporal relationships across manuscripts and inscriptions. Projects produce linked open data (IIIF manifests, structured metadata) that enable cross-text discovery while inheriting the reuse conditions of their underlying editions and archives.

title: Digitization
description: Digitization is the production of digital surrogates of manuscripts and inscriptions: high-resolution spectral (multi-/multi-spectral) imaging, metadata capture (Dublin Core, MODS), and optical character recognition (OCR/HTR) for scripts such as Devanāgarī, Grantha, and Tamil. Standards (FADGI 4-star, Metamorfoze, UNESCO) govern image quality and metadata; workflows include multispectral imaging of faded ink, crowdsourced transcription (e.g. via Wikisource), and IIIF delivery. The Digital India Library and Muktabodha host digitized Sanskrit texts and manuscripts; access must honor source copyright and cultural sensitivities.

title: Draupadī
description: Draupadi (द्रौप्य) is the Pāṇḍava wife, central to the Mahābhārata's central moral-legal crisis. The Dice Game in the Sabhā Parva, in which she is wagered and humiliated, triggers the war. Her vow never to bind her hair keeps it loose until the war's end. Her son Abhimanyu's birth and death frame the middle of the epic, and her later lament anchors the fall of the Kurus. She is the archetype of dharma under duress and the exemplary patient wife (pativrata).

title: Durgā Forms
description: The forms of Durgā: the nine Navadurgās (Śailaputrī, Brahmacāriṇī, Chandraghaṇṭā, Kūṣmāṇḍā, Skandamātā, Kātyāyanī, Kālarātrī, Mahāgaurī, Siddhidātrī); the ten Mahāvidyās; the warrior Caṇḍikā and the mother Ambikā.

title: Durgā
description: Durga (दुर्गा) is the fierce form of the Goddess who battles the buffalo-demon Mahiṣasura, as told in the Mārcarākṣa of the Devi-Māhābhārata and the Devi-Bhāgavata. She rides a lion and holds the discus, mace, lotus, and conch, and is worshipped at the autumn (Āsvina) festival of Durga Puja as the victory of consciousness over ego. Regional forms include Kālī and Badrakālī; her iconography is codified in dhyāna-slokas and she is the supreme Śakti worshiped across the goddess (Śākta) tradition.

title: Duryodhana
description: Duryodhana (दुर्यodhana) is the eldest Kaurava and the principal antagonist of the Mahābhārata, whose envy of the Pāṇḍavas triggers the Dice Game, the exile, and the Kurukshetra war. The narrative presents him through the lens of dharma (kṣatriya duty of rule): his strength is matched by moral blindness. He is ultimately undone by the destruction of his lineage; his fall exemplifies the triumph of righteousness over nepotism. His counsellors and his end are recounted in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam and the Mahābhārata's Śrīmadhāra section.

title: Dvaita Pañca-bheda
description: The Dvaita Vedānta doctrine of five eternal differences (pañca-bheda): between Brahman (Viṣṇu) and jīva, between Brahman and jagat, between jīva and jīva, between jīva and jagat, and between jagat and jagat.

title: Dvaita Sākṣi-bhāva
description: In Dvaita Vedānta, the sākṣi-bhāva (witness-consciousness) of the jīva is its capacity to witness its own mental states while remaining distinct from them.

title: Emendation
description: Emendation is an editorial intervention proposing a reading different from all extant witnesses when the tradition appears corrupt (homoeoteleuton, dittography, scribal errors). Classical criteria (the Latin 'difficilior potior' — prefer the harder reading, transcribe divine author) evaluate plausibility: a lectio difficilior, an internal coherence with context, and agreement with the author's style. In Sanskrit the apparatus also weighs metrical (chandas) and grammatical (vyākaraṇa) constraints. Emendations are siglated (* abbreviatio) and debated in secondary literature rather than silently imposed.

title: Epigraphy
description: The study of inscriptions on durable materials (stone, metal, copper plates) for historical, linguistic, and cultural reconstruction.

title: Folio
description: A folio (pakṣa) is one leaf of a manuscript, a physical artefact with two pages: recto (turned side) and verso (hair side). In Sanskrit palm-leaf manuscripts the folio is oriented vertically, paginated with red or black numerals, and sewn into quires (chhāyas); the term also denotes the folio-numbering system (e.g. 'folio 23 recto'). Catalogues (Muktabodha, Digital Index) record dimensions, condition, and foliation; the digital surrogate preserves each folio with IIIF deep-zoom so readers may inspect scribal corrections, stains, and marginalia without handling the original.

title: Gāndhārī
description: Gandhari (गांधारी) is the blind Kaurva queen, wife of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who voluntarily blinded herself to share her husband's condition. The Śānti Parva appoints her the repository of statecraft (rājādharma) and lamentation; the Vidura Smṛti and the Gandhārī-dhyāna preserve her precepts. She is mother of the hundred Kauravas and the voice of dynastic continuity; her lament for the war is among the epic's most moving passages.

title: Gaṇeśa Forms
description: The forms of Gaṇeśa: Bāl Gaṇeśa, Taruṇa Gaṇeśa, Bhakti Gaṇeśa, Vīra Gaṇeśa, Śakti Gaṇeśa, Dvija Gaṇeśa, Siddhi Gaṇeśa, Ucchiṣṭa Gaṇeśa, Vighna Gaṇeśa, Kṣipra Gaṇeśa, Heramba Gaṇeśa, and Lakṣmī Gaṇeśa.

title: Gāyatrī Mantra
description: The Gāyatrī Mantra (Ṛgveda 3.62.10), addressed to Savitṛ, is the most revered Vedic mantra.

title: Gāyatrī
description: The Gāyatrī (गायत्री) is the celebrated Vedic metre (twenty-four syllables of the Ṛg Veda 3.62.10) and its personified deity, invoked in the sandhyā of the twice-initiated. The Gāyatrī-mantra — oṃ bhūr bhuvanam... bhargo devasya dhīmahi — is the essence of the sandhyā-upāsanā and the Āraṇyaka, the pivot of brāhmaṇa ritual and the discipline of the atma-yajña. Recited with regulated breath and taught by the preceptor, it is the first mantra imparted to the initiated disciple.

title: Gītā Bhakti-yoga
description: The Bhagavad Gītā's teaching of bhakti-yoga (the yoga of devotion): the qualities of the devotee (bhakta), the nature of divine love, and the supremacy of bhakti as the path to liberation.

title: Gītā Dhyāna
description: The Bhagavad Gītā-dhyāna verses are the eight (or more) traditional opening stanzas recited before reading the Gītā, invoking the text's power and the grace of Kṛṣṇa and the āchāryas. Found in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam and other Purāṇas, they present the Gītā as the essence of the Upaniṣads, the Bhagavad-gītā as the destroyer of evil, and Śaṅkara, Rāmānuja, or KṚṣṇa-Caitanya as the commentarial source. The dhyāna establishes the liturgical (pāṭhaka) context: it is recited in the gurukula before śravaṇa and forms part of the traditional pūjā of the Gītā manuscript.

title: Gītā Jñāna-yoga
description: The Bhagavad Gītā's teaching of jñāna-yoga (the yoga of knowledge): the distinction between kṣetra (field) and kṣetrajña (knower of the field), the nature of the self (ātman), and the realization of brahman.

title: Gītā Karma-yoga
description: The Bhagavad Gītā's teaching of karma-yoga (the yoga of selfless action): niṣkāma-karma (action without attachment to fruits), svadharma (one's own duty), and the synthesis of action and knowledge.

title: Gītā Māhātmya
description: The Gītā-mahātmya ('glorification of the Gītā') is the genre of Purāṇic hymns extolling the Bhagavad Gītā as the foremost of spiritual science. The best-known (Vallabha's Bhāgavata-related version, the Anuvābhāṣikī) declares the Gītā superior to the Vedas and the Gītā-dhyāna of Sūta. These Mahātmyas are recited in the Gītā-purṇa-kathā and on Gītā-jayanti, and they encode a theological hierarchy (Īśvara → Gītā → guru → text). The Gītā-mahātmya literature thus mediates between scriptural authority and devotional practice, securing the text's ritual performance (patha, homa).

title: Guru-Śiṣya Paramparā
description: The guru-śiṣya paramparā (teacher-disciple lineage): the oral transmission of knowledge (vidyā) from guru to śiṣya across generations; its role in Vedic, Vedānta, Yoga, Tantra, and artistic traditions; the concepts of dīkṣā (initiation), śraddhā (faith), and the guru as the embodiment of the teaching.

title: Hanumān Forms
description: The forms of Hanumān (Añjanīputra, Māruti, Vāyusuta): the five-faced (pañcamukha) Hanumān, the eleven Rudra manifestations, the vīra (heroic) and dāsya (servitude) aspects.

title: Hanumān
description: Hanumān (हनुमान्) is the vānara (forest-being) and devoted servant of Rāma in the Vālmiki Rāmāyaṇa and the Sundara Kāṇḍa, the son of the wind-god. He leaps to Lanka, finds Sītā, and burns the city; he is the embodiment of service (sevā) and devotion (bhakti). Worshipped on Hanumān Jayantī in the month of Kārtika, he is the remover of obstacles (vighna-hara) and protector of thresholds. His iconography (mace, mountain, simian form) is set in dhyāna-slokas and his name ends many a sādhaka's practice.

title: Hare Kṛṣṇa Mahāmantra
description: The Hare Kṛṣṇa mahāmantra is the congregational (saṅkīrtana) mantra of the Gauḍīya tradition, composed of the names Hare, Kṛṣṇa, and Rāma arranged as: hare kṛṣṇa hare kṛṣṇa kṛṣṇa kṛṣṇa / hare rāma hare rāma rāma rāma hare hare — the 32-syllable (16-word) mantra addressed to the divine feminine energy (Hare), the all-attractive supreme (Kṛṣṇa), and his pleasure (Rāma). Caitanya Mahāprabhu (1486–1533) is said to have propounded it as the supreme practice (śuddha-nāma-saṅkīrtana) for the age of Kali, receiving it in the spiritual line descending from Śrī Caitanya's own guru (Lochmānadāsa Gosvāmī → Nārāyaṇa Gauḍa).

title: Hindustani Gharānā
description: The Hindustani gharanā (lineage/school) system: the major vocal gharanās (Gwalior, Agra, Jaipur-Atrauli, Kirana, Patiala, Bhendi Bazaar, Indore, Mewati, Rampur-Sahaswan) and instrumental gharanās (Imdadkhani/Etawah sitar, Maihar sarod, etc.).

title: Īśvara
description: Īśvara (ईश्वर) is the personal Lord, the soteriological ground in the Āstika Darśanas, understood variously as the creator, the author of the Vedas (svayaṃ-śruti), and the object of devotion (bhakti). In Yoga (Patañjali 1.23) Īśvara is a special puruṣa (viśeṣa) free from karma; in Vedānta Īśvara is Brahman immanent as the causal (sarvāntara) and efficient cause. The Gītā (9.2) calls Īśvara the source of the Gītā itself. The Īśvara-praṇidhāna (surrender to the Lord) is a limb of Yoga and a gateway of bhakti.

title: Itihāsa Saṃskāra
description: The cultural impact of the Itihāsas (Mahābhārata and Rāmāyaṇa) on Indian civilization: their role in shaping values, performing arts (Kathakali, Yakṣagāṇa, Rāmalīlā), temple iconography, regional languages, and the transmission of dharma across generations.

title: Jaiminīya Śākhā
description: The Jaiminīya Śākhā (also Talavakāra Śākhā) is a recension of the Sāmaveda, prevalent in South India; its texts include the Jaiminīya Saṃhitā, Brāhmaṇa, Āraṇyaka, and Upaniṣad.

title: Japa Mālā
description: Japa mālā (prayer beads, mala) is a string of 108 beads (plus one larger guru-bead, the 'sumihira' / 'meru') used to count repetitions of a mantra or divine name during japa. Traditionally made of Tulsi (holy basil) wood or rudrakṣa (divine-eye) seeds, it is held in the right hand and moved between the thumb and the other fingers, with the gaze averted, to aid sustained concentration on the sacred syllable or name.

title: Jīvanmukti
description: Jīvanmukti (जीवन्मुक्ति, 'liberation while living') is the highest attainment in Advaita and the other Vedāntas, in contrast to videhamukti (liberation after death). Śaṅkara defines it as the removal of the false superimposition (adhyāsa) by the means of knowledge (jñāna) — the realized sage (jīvanmukta) who is liberated while still embodied and moves in the world as the 'child of fortune' (saṃsāra). The text (Gītā 2.72, the Kathopananiṣad) describes the jīvanmukta as the 'great-souled' (mahātmā) whose conduct (caraṇa) transcends the guṇas.

title: Jñāna
description: Jñāna (ज्ञान) is discriminative knowledge that removes the veil of māyā and reveals the identity of ātman and Brahman, the means of liberation in the jñāna-mārga. Śaṅkara locates jñāna in the teachings (upaniṣad-vākya) transmitted through the paramparā and validated by śravaṇa (listening), manana (reflection), and nididhyāsana (meditative absorption). The Gītā's jñāna-yoga (chapters 2, 13, 15) distinguishes higher (para) knowledge (Brahma-jñāna) from lower (aparā) knowledge (the five elements and Vedas). In the Buddhist tradition jñāna is non-conceptual; in Vedānta it is counted among the three Puruṣārtha sādhāṇas alongside karma and bhakti.

title: Jyotiṣa
description: Jyotiḥśāstra (astronomy/astrology) is the Vedāṅga of celestial timekeeping (tithi, muhūrta, rāhu, yoginī, nakṣatra) regulating the ritual calendar and election of auspicious moments (muhūrta). The Taittirīya (Āraṣṭabhāṣini) and the Brāhmapurāṇa codify the nakṣatra (27/28) system, the motion of the planets (graha), and the timing of festivals; the Siddhānta tradition (Āryabhaṭa, Brahmagupta) later integrated Greek and Islamic elements. As a Vedāṅga it is a liminal discipline: timekeeping (the 'outer' jyotiṣa) for ritual and the horoscopic/astrological (the 'inner') for divination and life-timing.

title: Kalpa
description: Kalpa is the third Vedāṅga, the manual of ritual procedure (śrauta and gṛhya rites) prescribing the correct form, sequence, and utensils of sacrificial and domestic ceremonies, derived from the Brāhmaṇas. The Sūtra form (Shrauta-sūtras of Apastamba, Baudhayana, Āpastamba; Gṛhya-sūtras) renders the Brāhmaṇa prescriptions operational. The six Kalpa-sūtras (Āpastamba, Baudhāyana, etc.) were the most quoted and transmitted Vedāṅga and supplied the liturgical grammar for the later Dharmaśāstra and manual literature. Kalpa defines dharma as practice (acara) embedded in ritual performance.

title: Kāma
description: Kāma (काम) is desire and the erotic, the third of the four Puruṣārthas, the vital force that animates embodied life. The Kāma-sūtra (Vātsyāyana) and the Kāma-saṅgraha systematize the art of love, the stages of courtship, and the social arts. In the Gītā (2.45) kāma is part of the worldly three (triguṇa-viṣaya) that bind the self; yet in its right place (dharma-saṃyukta) it is a legitimate aim and the companion of artha and mokṣa. The Kāma-sūtra's seven parts are the classic schema of the arts of love.

title: Kāṇva Śākhā
description: The Kāṇva Śākhā is a principal recension of the Śukla (White) Yajurveda; its texts include the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā (Kāṇva recension), Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (Kāṇva), and Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (Kāṇva).

title: Kāpiṣṭhala Śākhā
description: The Kāpiṣṭhala Śākha (or Kāṭhaka) is a lesser recension (śākha) of the Black (Kṛṣṇa) Yajur Veda, closely related to the Kāṭha Śākha and known from the Kāpiṣṭhala Gṛhya-sūtra and an Āraṇyaka, both partially preserved. It is one of the surviving śākhas of the Yajur Veda and is cited in the Dharmaśāstras for certain life-cycle rites (e.g. the sacred-thread ceremony).

title: Karma
description: Karma (कर्म) literally 'action,' denotes in Indian thought the universal law of moral causation in which volitional action conditions future experience across lifetimes. The Gītā classifies karma as sañcita (accumulated), prārabdha (begun), and āgāmi (future), teaching karmayoga — action performed without attachment to results (niṣkāma karma) and as a means of purification (karmaśuddhi). The Vedic ritual karmas are distinguished from the ethical karmaphala of the Buddhist and Jain teachings. Liberation (mokṣa) requires the cessation of karmic bondage (karma-bandhana) through jñāna, bhakti, or yoga.

title: Karṇa
description: Karṇa (कर्ण) the 'ear-rings' hero is the forgotten son of Kunti (by Sūrya), raised by the charioteer-couple, and the champion of the Kauravas — the 'friend' of Duryodhana and the foil of Arjuna (his rival in arms and in dharma). The Mahābhārata (Karṇa and Śalya Parvas) depicts his unmatched generosity (dātṛtā) and the 'golden' (kanīnī) ear-rings of Virūpākṣa, his martial prowess (the 'head-to-head' fight with Arjuna), and his death by Arjuna's arrow while mounted (śiraḥ-stabdhāḥ). His tragedy is the tension between birth (jāti) and merit (karma).

title: Kaṭha Śākhā
description: The Kāṭha Śākha (Kāṭha) is a recension of the Black (Kṛṣṇa) Yajur Veda, the source of the Kāṭha Saṃhitā, the Kāṭha Brāhmaṇa, the Kāṭha Āraṇyaka, and the Kāṭha Upaniṣad (the Upaniṣad of Death, the dialogue between Naciketas and Yama). It is one of the surviving śākhas of the Yajur Veda; its texts preserve the 'death' (mṛtyu) doctrine and the early 'knowledge' (jñāna) of the Self (Ātman) that are central to the Vedānta.

title: Kathakali Vesham
description: The Kathakali vesham (makeup/costume) classification: paccā (green, noble/heroic), kaṭṭi (knife, anti-heroic), kari (black, demonic), teṭṭa (beard, ascetic), minukku (polished, female/sage).

title: Kauthuma Śākhā
description: The Kauthuma Śākhā is the principal surviving recension of the Sāmaveda; its texts include the Sāmaveda Saṃhitā, Chāndogya Brāhmaṇa, Chāndogya Upaniṣad, and Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa.

title: Kṛṣṇa Forms
description: The forms of Kṛṣṇa: the infant Bāla Gopāla, the cowherd Gopīnātha, the flute-player Veṇugopāla, the cow-lifter Govardhana-dhārī, the charioteer Pārtha-sārathi, the universal form Viśvarūpa, and the supreme Parabrahman.

title: Kṛṣṇa
description: KṚṣṇa (कृष्ण) is the black (śyāma) avatar of Viṣṇu (Vāsudeva) and the silent author of the Bhagavad Gītā. The Bhāgavata Purāṇa and Harivaṃśa present him as the Vṛndāvana cowherd, the ruler of Dvārakā, and the charioteer of Arjuna. His teaching of līlā (divine play), kāma as divine love, and the synthesis of jñāna, karma, and bhakti in the Gītā make him the pivot of the Vaiṣṇṇava theological tradition. His stories (Govardhana, Kaliya) and his counsel define the bhakti corpus.

title: Kuntī
description: Kunti (कुन्ती) is the Pāṇḍava mother, a Yādava princess married to the blind king Dhṛtarāṣṭra's brother, and foster-mother to Kṛṣṇa. The epic's early section recounts her boon — Kṛṣṇa as her son — and her later reunion with Karna, her firstborn. The Kunti-stotra and the Karṇa-parva preserve her voice of maternal grief and resolve; her patience (dhairya) and devotion to Kṛṣṇa (bhakti) are central themes of the epic's ethics of suffering (duḥkha).

title: Lakṣmaṇa
description: Lakṣmāṇa (लक्ष्मण) is the younger brother and constant companion of Rāma in the Vālmiki Rāmāyaṇa, the embodiment of faithful service (sevaka-dharma). He builds the bridge (setu-bandha) to Lanka, guards Sītā in the forest, and is the interlocutor of the Yuddha-kāṇḍa's counsel. He is worshipped as a patron of learning, and his loyalty (niyati) and resourcefulness (upāya) are the model of the ideal companion (saṃgāyitr) in epic and literature.

title: Lakṣmī Forms
description: The eight principal forms of Lakṣmī (Aṣṭalakṣmī): Ādi, Dhana, Dhānya, Gaja, Santāna, Vīra, Vijaya, and Vidyā.

title: Lakṣmī
description: Lakṣmī (लक्ष्मी) is the goddess of prosperity and auspiciousness, the principal consort (śakti) of Viṣṇu/Nārāyaṇa. Born in the churning of the ocean (samudra-manthan) as the daughter of the Ocean, she is the four-fold Lakṣmī: Sīdhārthī, Gajalakṣmī, Mahālakṣmī, and Padma-lakṣmī. She is the focus of Diwali worship (Lakṣmī-pūjā) and appears in the Sākambhalīṇi and the Padma-Purāṇa. She is depicted holding lotus, conch, discus, and book.

title: Lalitā Sahasranāma
description: The Lālita-sahasranāma ('Thousand Names of the Goddess Lālita') is a stotra that eulogizes the supreme goddess Lālita (Tripurasundarī) as the dynamic (śakti) emanation of Śiva. It occurs in the Brahmanda Purāṇa (in the section dealing with the goddess) and is structured as a series of thousand names arranged in groups that progressively describe her physical form, her entourage (the yogīs, the ḍākinīs), her ornaments, her vahanas (the bull, the billy-goat), and her martial/iconographic attributes, ending with the doctrinal statement of non-duality (advaita).

title: Mādhyandina Śākhā
description: The Mādhyandina Śākhā is a principal recension of the Śukla (White) Yajurveda, prevalent in North India; its texts include the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, and Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.

title: Mahā Mrityunjaya Mantra
description: The Mahāmṛtyuñjaya Mantra — tryambakaṃ yajāmahe... sarvapāpeha (Ṛg Veda 7.59.12 to Tryambaka) — is the pre-eminent Śaiva invocation for longevity, healing, and deliverance from untimely death. It is recited in the Rudra-abhiṣeka on Mahaśiva Rātri and is the 'king of hymns' (sūkta-rajju). The Gauḍīya tradition pairs it with the Hare-Kṛṣṇa mahā-mantra as a sādhana of heart's deliverance (hṛdaya-mukti); it is the verse of the Sandarbhas (kāyānta).

title: Mahābhārata Principal Characters
description: The principal characters of the Mahābhārata: the Pāṇḍavas (Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma, Arjuna, Nakula, Sahadeva), the Kauravas (Duryodhana and his brothers), Kṛṣṇa, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa, Draupadī, and others.

title: Mahābhārata Parvas
description: The eighteen parvas (books) of the Mahābhārata: Ādi, Sabhā, Araṇya, Virāṭa, Udyoga, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa, Śalya, Sauptika, Strī, Śānti, Anuśāsana, Āśramavāsika, Mausala, Mahāprasthānika, Svargārohaṇa.

title: Mahābhārata Upaniṣads
description: A group of Upaniṣads embedded in the Mahābhārata, including the Mokṣa-dharma-parvan and the Bhagavad Gītā context.

title: Mahābhārata War
description: The Kurukṣetra War, the central conflict of the Mahābhārata, fought between the Pāṇḍavas and Kauravas over eighteen days.

title: Mahāpurāṇa
description: The Mahāpurāṇa ('Great Purāṇa') refers to the eighteen major Purāṇas (e.g. Vishnu, Śiva, Devi, Bhāgavata) distinguished from the Upapurāṇas by their broader scope, earlier strata, and fuller treatment of the pañcalakṣaṇa (five features). They preserve the theological synthesis of the śruti-smṛti, genealogies (vaṃśa), cosmology (kalpa), and the avatars of Viṣṇu across myth and history. The Bhāgavata is the exemplar. The Mahāpurāṇas are also a textual group: their redactors (the 'five brāhmaṇas') and regional recensions vary; the Padma and Vāyu preserve variant genealogies used by historians of Indian religious art.

title: Maitrāyaṇīya Śākhā
description: The Maitrāyaṇīya Śākha is a recension of the White (Śukla) Yajur Veda, the source of the Maitrāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, Brāhmaṇa, Āraṇyaka, and Upaniṣad. The Śākha preserves the 'three cities' (triloka) doctrine of the Self and is notable for the 'mind' (manas) and the 'breath' (prāṇa) passages that influenced the Buddhist and Jain psychology of the mind. The Maitrāyaṇīya Upaniṣad is one of the 'minor' (upaniṣad) sources for the doctrine of the inner (antarātman) versus the outer (bāhira) self.

title: Mandodarī
description: Māndodarī (मांदोदरी) is the chaste queen of Rāvaṇa in the Rāmāyaṇa, the 'wide-bellied' (maudodarya) queen of Laṅkā and the voice of conscience to her husband. The Sundara Kāṇḍa records her warning (the 'consequences of war' against Rāma) and her lament at the death of her son Indrajit (Meghanāḍa). She is the archetype of the wise and patient queen (rāṇī) and the faithful wife (patnī), and her counsel that 'Rāma's victory is at hand' marks the turning of the Lanka-episode.

title: Manuscript Catalogue
description: A systematic descriptive record of manuscript holdings, including codicological, paleographical, and textual metadata.

title: Manuscript Preservation
description: The preventive and remedial conservation of manuscripts: environmental control, housing, handling, and treatment.

title: Māyāvāda
description: Māyā-vāda ('the doctrine of illusion') asserts that the phenomenal world is māyā (unreal appearance) in relation to the absolute Brahman. The term is used polemically by the Bauddhas and as a label for Advaita by its critics (Madhva, the Mīmāṃsakas), who object that it trivializes the reality of the world and the agency of the deity. Advaitins prefer the more precise 'vivarta-vāda' (apparent transformation): māyā is anirvacanīya (indescribable), the superimposition (adhyāsa) of the real upon the unreal, removed by jñāna rather than denied as inert.

title: Māyā
description: Māyā (माया) is the creative power or projective illusion that conceals Brahman as the phenomenal world, the central problem of Advaita Vedānta. Śaṅkara describes māyā as anirvacanīya ('indescribable') — like rope mistaken for a snake — neither existent nor non-existent. The Gītā (9.38–40) attributes the world's appearance to māyā as the womb of the worlds; the doctrine grounds Advaita's epistemology (only Brahman is real, all else is mithyā dependent on Brahman) and the doctrine of adhyāsa (superimposition).

title: Mīmāṃsā Apūrva
description: The Mīmāṃsā concept of apūrva (the unseen potency generated by ritual action that produces future fruits).

title: Mīmāṃsā Arthavāda
description: The Mīmāṃsā theory of arthavāda (explanatory passages in the Veda): the classification of Vedic sentences into vidhi (injunction), nṣedha (prohibition), and arthavāda (explanation).

title: Mīmāṃsā Dharma
description: The Mīmāṃsā conception of dharma as ritual duty prescribed by the Veda, known through śabda pramāṇa (verbal testimony).

title: Mīmāṃsā Sphoṭa
description: The Mīmāṃsā theory of sphoṭa (the eternal, unchanging word-essence) as the bearer of meaning, distinct from the audible sound (dhvani); the debate between Kumārila Bhaṭṭa (who rejects sphoṭa) and the Grammarians (who affirm it).

title: Mokṣa
description: Mokṣa (मोक्ष) is liberation from the cycle of birth and death (saṃsāra) and the cessation of karmic bondage, the final of the four puruṣārthas. The Darśanas offer divergent formulations: Ādi Śaṅkara defines it as jīvanmukti — the realization that ātman is Brahman, accomplished in life; Rāmānuja locates it in eternal loving service (prema) to Nārāyaṇa; Madhva in eternal distinction between soul and God. The Gītā presents jñāna, karma, and bhakti mārgas as convergences toward mokṣa. Mokṣa is variously temporal (jīvanmukti) and ultimate (paramukti), with Śaiva and Buddhist variants as ātura-jñāna and nirvāṇa respectively.

title: Murugaṇ Forms
description: The forms of Murugaṇ (Kārttikeya, Subrahmaṇya, Skanda): the six-faced Ṣaṇmukha, the youthful Kumāra, the warrior Senāpati, the Tamil deity of the Kurinji landscape; the six abodes (Arupadai Veedu: Tiruttani, Swamimalai, Palani, Tirupparankunram, Pazhamudircholai, Tiruchendur).

title: Navagraha
description: The Navagraha (nine celestial influencers): Sūrya (Sun), Candra (Moon), Maṅgala (Mars), Budha (Mercury), Bṛhaspati (Jupiter), Śukra (Venus), Śani (Saturn), Rāhu (ascending node), Ketu (descending node).

title: Nirukta
description: Nirukta, the Vedāṅga of etymology and interpretation traditionally ascribed to Yāska (6th c. BCE), explains the meaning of archaic and ambiguous words, especially Vedic hymn-names and vocables, by deriving them from roots (dhātu) and analyzing compounds (samāsa). Its method (nirukta) balances the phonetic (śabda) with the semantic (artha) and distinguishes the established usage (kāraṇa) from the speculative (tātparya-vacana). It preserves some of the oldest native linguistic thinking (the 'three' vowels, the derivation of proper names) and anchors the Brāhmana and Prātiśākhya interpretation of the Vedic corpus.

title: Numismatics
description: Numismatics is the study of coins (Tāmra-śāstra) and other monetary and stamp impressions (tāmra-patra) as historical and economic evidence. In India the field spans punch-marked coins (1st millennium BCE) through the silver karshapanas of the Gupta age, the gold dinars of the Gurjara-Pratihara and the Chola, and the inscribed copper-plates (tāmra-patra) recording land grants. Numismatic evidence dates texts and monuments, reveals trade networks, and identifies issuer-legends (devanām pāla-karaṇḍavaha). Catalogues (Mukherjee, Singh) and hoard-studies anchor regional chronologies.

title: Nyāya Hetvābhāsa
description: The Nyāya classification of fallacies of inference (hetvābhāsas) including savyabhicāra, viruddha, satpratipakṣa, asiddha, and bādhita.

title: Nyāya Īśvara
description: The Nyāya concept of Īśvara (God) as the efficient cause (nimitta-kāraṇa) of the universe, the creator, sustainer, and destroyer of the world, who is distinct from the material cause (prakṛti) and the individual selves (jīva).

title: Nyāya Pramāṇas
description: The Nyāya school recognizes four pramāṇas (means of valid knowledge): pratyakṣa (perception), anumāna (inference), upamāna (comparison), and śabda (verbal testimony).

title: Nyāya Siddhānta
description: The Nyāya school's core doctrines: the sixteen padārthas (categories) including pramāṇa (means of knowledge), prameya (objects of knowledge), saṃśaya (doubt), prayojana (purpose), dṛṣṭānta (example), siddhānta (tenet), avayava (members of inference), tarka (reasoning), nirṇaya (ascertainment), vāda (discussion), jalpa (wrangling), vitaṇḍā (cavil), hetvābhāsa (fallacies), chala (quibble), jāti (futile objection), and nigrahasthāna (point of defeat).

title: Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya
description: Oṃ namaḥ Śivāya (Om Namah Shivaya), popularly called the Pañcākṣara ('five syllables') mantra — Oṃ + namaḥ + śi + vā + ya — is a principal Śaiva mantra addressed to Śiva. The five syllables are identified with the five primordial elements (pañca-bhūta) and the five faces (pañca-mukha) of Śiva; with the bija 'Oṃ' (the supreme sound) and 'namaḥ' (prostration), the mantra is traditionally recited 108 times and is regarded in the Śaiva Siddhānta as a direct sādhana to dissolve the sense of ego and merge in Śiva.

title: Oṃ Namo Nārāyaṇāya
description: Oṃ Namo Nārāyaṇāya is the traditional eight-syllable aṣṭākṣara invocation of Viṣṇu/Bhagavān, cited in the Ṛg Veda, the Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad, and the Divya Prabandham. It is the core dhyāna-sādhana of the Vaiṣṇṇava traditions (Gauḍīya, Śrīvaiṣṇava, Dvaita), the heart of the Nārāyaṇa-mantra, and recited in the sandhyā and the Gītā-pūjā. The eight syllables unfold the progression from the embodied self to the supreme Nārāyaṇa, and are the formula of safe conclusion (sukhānta) taught at the deathbed.

title: Oṃ
description: Oṃ (ॐ) is the praṇava, the primordial syllable, the sound-form of the absolute from which the Vedas and all phenomena are said to arise and dissolve. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka and the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣads (oṃ ity etad akṣara) present oṃ as bow, the self as the arrow, Brahman as the target. Its three sounds (a-u-m) correspond to waking, dream, and deep-sleep, and the fourth (parā, turīya) the transcendent state beyond the three. It opens every Vedic and tantric act and is the object of japa and dhyāna.

title: Padma Tīrtha
description: Padma-tīrtha (the 'lotus-tīrtha') is a sacred pilgrimage site associated with the lotus (padma) of Viṣṇu, most notably the sacred pool at Vārāṇasī (Kāśī) where the Ganga is said to descend and the lotus-navel of Nārāyaṇa (Viṣṇu) is bathed. The padma-tirtha is the 'lotus-place' (padma-sthala) for the rites of the dead (antyeṣṭi) and for the removal of sins (pāpa) and the birth in Kāśī. It is distinct from the Padmanābha temple of Travancore.

title: Paippalāda Śākhā
description: The Paippalāda Śākhā is a recension of the Atharvaveda, historically prominent in Kashmir and Odisha; its Saṃhitā is partially preserved and differs from the Śaunaka recension.

title: Paleography
description: Paleography (lekhā-śāstra) is the discipline of dating and localizing scripts from their letter-forms (akṣara) and writing habits (ligatures, rephas, anusvāra). In India the script-family (Brāhmī → Gupta → Devanāgarī, Grantha, Tibetan, Śāradā, etc.) is branched by the 4th c. BCE, with each script regionally diversified (e.g. Nāgārjunakonda, Gilgit). Paleography anchors datation of undated manuscripts and inscriptions; standards (Girard, Salomon) correlate letter-form evolution with political chronology and monastic centres of scribal production.

title: Pañcamahābhūta
description: The five great elements (pañcamahābhūta) in Vedic and Sāṃkhya cosmology: ākāśa (space/ether), vāyu (air), agni (fire), jala/ap (water), pṛthvī (earth).

title: Pariṇāmavāda
description: Pariṇāmavāda — the theory of (real) transformation — holds that the effect pre-exists in its material cause and arises as a real change of that substance, the doctrine of Sāṃkhya-Yoga and the Gītā (2.45: all beings arise from and return to the elements). It opposes Advaita's vivarta-vāda (apparent transformation) and the Buddhist theory of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda). The doctrine underwrites the karmic account of rebirth and the Sāṃkhya causal theory (Satkāryavāda) that what exists cannot be produced from nothing.

title: Prakṛti
description: Prakṛti (प्रकृति) is primordial matter or nature, the source of the material universe in Sāṃkhya and the field (kṣetra) of Puruṣa-consciousness in the Gītā (13.19–20). From the equilibrium of the three Guṇas (sattva, rajas, tamas) Prakṛti differentiates into the Mahābhūtas (five great elements) and from them the ten Mahābhūtas-digāma indriyas, forming the subtle and gross bodies that bind Puruṣa. Kālāmsa's Sāṃkhyakārikā defines Prakṛti as the matrix of the twenty-five tattvas (mahābhūta up to abuddha). Liberation (mokṣa) is the cessation of this material manifestation through the discriminative knowledge (vivekanābhyāsa) that Puruṣa is distinct from Prakṛti.

title: Prasthānatraya
description: The Prasthāna-traya ('the three sources/canon') is the text-corpus of the Vedānta: the Upaniṣads (Prasthāna, the 'scriptural' source), the Brahma-sūtras (Nyāya, the 'reasoning' source), and the Bhagavad Gītā (Smṛti, the 'traditional' source). Śaṅkara's bhāṣyas on the trio are the foundation of the Advaita system; each Vedānta school (Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita, Dvaita, Śuddhādvaita, Gauḍīya) takes the trio as its starting point (prasthāna) and reconciles its teaching.

title: Prāyaścitta Types
description: The classification of prāyaścitta (expiation) in Dharmaśātra: prāṇāyāma, tīrtha-yātrā, dāna, vrata, homa, japa, and fasting.

title: Prāyaścitta
description: Prayāsa-cchita (प्रायश्चित्त) is the Dharmaśāstra genre of expiatory rites for intentional or incidental transgressions, performed by the 'means of cleansing' (√yaj, √śam). The Smṛtis enumerate the expiations: penance (tapas), bathing (snāna), feeding the Brāhmana (anna-dāna), recitation of the Gāyatrī, and the 'great' expiations (e.g. three days of fasting). Their form (karma) varies by caste (varṇa) and by the severity of the offense; the Gītā (4.13) frames expiation as the restoration of dharma.

title: Pūjā Ṣoḍaśopacāra
description: The sixteen upacāras (offerings) in formal Pūjā: āvāhana (invocation), āsana (seat), pādyā (water for feet), arghya (water for hands), ācamana (sipping water), snāna (bath), vastra (clothing), yajñopavīta (sacred thread), gandha (sandalwood), puṣpa (flowers), dhūpa (incense), dīpa (lamp), naivedya (food), tāmbūla (betel), nīrājana (waving lights), and mantra-puṣpāñjali.

title: Mahāpurāṇa List
description: The eighteen Mahāpurāṇas: Brahma, Padma, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Liṅga, Garuḍa, Nārada, Bhāgavata, Agni, Skanda, Bhaviṣya, Brahmāṇḍa, Vāmana, Kūrma, Matsya, Vāyu, Varāha, and Vāyu.

title: Purāṇa Pañcalakṣaṇa
description: The Pañcalakṣaṇa ('five marks') are the defining characteristics by which a text is recognized as a Purāṇa: (1) Sarga — creation and emanation of beings; (2) Pratisarga — re-creation or the destruction and renewed activity of the cosmos; (3) Vaṃśa — genealogies of kings (solar and lunar) and of the ādikartas; (4) Manvantara — the reigns of the fourteen Manu-s, and the avatāras of Viṣṇu; (5) Vaṃśānucarita — the deeds of the royal dynasties (e.g., the Raghu-vaṃśa). These five topoi organize the narrative frame of the Mahāpurāṇa corpus and distinguish Purāṇic from Mahābhārata and itihāsa composition styles.

title: Purāṇa Sectarian Classification
description: The traditional tripartite classification of Purāṇas by predominance of guṇas: Sāttvika (Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa), Rājasa (Brahmā), and Tāmasa (Śiva).

title: Purāṇa Structure
description: The five characteristic topics (pañcalakṣaṇa) of the Purāṇas: sarga (creation), pratisarga (secondary creation), vaṃśa (genealogies), manvantara (cosmic cycles), and vaṃśānucarita (dynastic histories).

title: Purāṇa Traditional Attribution
description: Traditional attribution assigns the major Purāṇas to Vyāsa as compiler; this attribution is represented here as a traditional claim distinct from modern textual scholarship on Purāṇa composition and stratification. ---

title: Upapurāṇas
description: The eighteen Upapurāṇas (minor Purāṇas): Saura, Nṛsiṃha, Viṣṇu Dharmottara, Kālikā, Garga, Āditya, Nandi, Sāmba, Nṛsiṃha Tāpanīya, Bhārgava, Matsya, Varāha, Kapila, Mānava, Auśanasa, Sāmba, Nṛsiṃha Tāpanīya, and Bhārgava.

title: Puruṣa
description: Puruṣa (पुरुष) is the conscious principle, the pure spirit or self distinct from matter (Prakṛti). In the Ṛg Veda (Puruṣa Sūkta) Puruṣa is the cosmic person sacrificed by the gods to create the four varṇas. In the Sāṃkhya system Puruṣa is singular (ekānta) while prakṛti is plural-principled; the multiplicity of individual puruṣas is denied by Śaṅkara (ātman as Puruṣa). The Kathopananiṣad distinguishes the embodied puruṣa (kāmaccara) from the liberated. Liberation is Puruṣa's recognition of its aloofness (viyuktatva) from prakāśa-vimarda.

title: Puruṣārtha
description: Puruṣārtha (पुरुषार्थ) is the doctrine of the four aims of human life — dharma (righteousness), artha (wealth), kāma (desire), and mokṣa (liberation) — the framework organizing Hindu ethical and spiritual life across the Āstika Darśanas and the Dharmaśāstras. The four-fold classification appears explicitly in the later Dharmaśāstras (e.g., Manu Smṛti) and is interpreted differently across schools: the Mīmāṃsā elevates dharma, the Yoga its synthesis, the Vedānta subordinates the worldly three (triguṇa-vairāgya) to mokṣa. Their mutual priority is a perennial point of tension (dharma-artha-kāmeṣu virōdhāḥ).

title: Rājadharma
description: The Dharmaśāstra conception of rājadharma (kingly duties): the king's role as protector of varṇāśrama-dharma, the principles of just rule (daṇḍanīti), taxation, justice, and the ideal of the cakravartin.

title: Rāma Forms
description: The forms of Rāma: the prince of Ayodhyā, the exiled forest-dweller, the victor over Rāvaṇa, the ideal king (Rāmarājya), and the supreme Parabrahman (in Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa).

title: Rāma
description: Rāma (राम) is the hero (puruṣottama) of the Vālmiki Rāmāyaṇa, the ikṣvāku prince exiled to the forest, husband of Sītā and brother of Bharata and Lakṣmāṇa. The epic (Bāla to Yuddha) stages the ideal of dharma through the conflict between duty and family (his abandonment of Sītā). His coronation after the war establishes the ideal of Rāma-rājya — righteous kingship — and he is later worshipped as the mūrti of bhakti and the exemplar of the ideal son, husband, and king. The Rāmcharitamanas and the regional Rāmāyaṇas preserve his cult.

title: Rāmāyaṇa Principal Characters
description: The principal characters of the Rāmāyaṇa: Rāma, Sītā, Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata, Śatrughna, Hanumān, Sugrīva, Vibhīṣaṇa, Rāvaṇa, and others.

title: Rāmāyaṇa Kāṇḍas
description: The Kāṇḍas (books) of the Vālmiki Rāmāyaṇa are seven: Bāla, Ayodhyā, Āraṇya, Kiṣkindhā, Sundara, Yuddha, and Uttara (the later). The Bāla tells Rāma's birth; Ayodhya the exile (bhrammaṇa); Āraṇya the forest (vana-vāsa); Kiṣkindhā the search (siddha) with Hanumān and the vanaras; Sundara the finding (sphurana) of Sītā in Lanka; Yuddha the war (the 'great war' of Rāma vs. Rāvaṇa); Uttara Rāma's coronation and the birth of the next generation (Lava-Kūla and the Rāma-setu).

title: Rāmāyaṇa Philosophy
description: The philosophical and ethical teachings of the Rāmāyaṇa: the ideals of dharma (righteousness), satya (truth), kṣamā (forgiveness), dayā (compassion), and the ideal ruler (Rāma-rājya).

title: Rāṇāyanīya Śākhā
description: The Rāṇāyanīya Śākhā is a recension of the Sāmaveda, historically prominent in Gujarat and Maharashtra; its texts are closely related to the Kauthuma recension.

title: Rasa Siddhānta
description: Rasa (रस) is the aesthetic sentiment, the 'flavour' evoked in the audience by art, systematized in the Nāṭyaśāstra as the eight primary rasas: śṛṅgāra (love), hāsya (humour), karuṇa (compassion), raudra (anger), vīra (heroism), bhayānaka (terror), bībhatsa (disgust), adbhuta (wonder); with śānta added in the later tradition. The theory (rasa-siddhānta), developed by Abhinavagupta, is the aesthetic counterpart to devotion (bhāva); rasa is the relish (āsvāda) of the fully-experienced emotion. The conditions (ālambana, ātmikā, vibhāvya) and the nine rasas structure classical Sanskrit poetics and the performing arts (nṛtya).

title: Rāvaṇa
description: Rāvaṇ(a) (रावण, 'the captive') is the ten-headed (daśa-sira) king of Laṅkā, the Rākṣasa who abducts Sītā and is the central antagonist of the Vālmiki Rāmāyaṇa. His ten heads are traditionally the ten organs (indriyas) and the ten directions, the symbol of pride (aṭṭā) and the 'over-reacher' who, despite his learning (śāstra) and boons (vara), is undone by lust (kāma) and the curse (śapatha). The Rāmāyaṇa stages his defeat (vijaya) as the triumph of dharma (dharma) over the demonic (āsura).

title: Recension
description: A distinct version or redaction of a text transmitted in a particular geographical, textual, or institutional tradition.

title: Ṛgveda Śākhās
description: The recensions (śākhās) of the Ṛgveda: the Śākalya śākhā (the only complete surviving recension), and historically attested lost recensions such as Bāṣkala, Āśvalāyana, Śāṅkhāyana, and Māṇḍukeya.

title: Ṛṇa-trayā
description: The three debts (ṛṇa-traya) in Dharmaśāstra: ṛṣi-ṛṇa (debt to sages, repaid by study), deva-ṛṇa (debt to gods, repaid by sacrifice), pitṛ-ṛṇa (debt to ancestors, repaid by progeny).

title: Ṛṇa
description: Ṛṇa (ऋण) is debt or obligation, a fundamental principle in Indian thought whereby the individual owes debts (ṛṇa) to the cosmos, gods, sages, ancestors, and fellow humans. The concept is articulated in the Gītā (17.14) and elaborated in the Ṛg Veda (e.g., the Gāyatrī-ṛṇa) and the Dharmaśāstras. Repayment (ṛṇa-nivṛtti) is through progeny (putrārtham), study (śrāddha), and ritual (yajña), culminating in liberation when the debts are discharged. The Buddhist conception of anattā rejects ṛṇa as a permanent self-debtor, while the Jain aṇuvañcana counts ṛṇa-kṣaya (debt-diminishment) among the attributes of a liberated being.

title: Śrī Rudram
description: The Śrī Rudram (Rudra-praṇālī) is the most celebrated hymn to Rudra-Śiva in the Śukla (white) Yajurveda, occurring as the Taittirīya Saṃhita (VS) 4.1–10 and its Āraṇyaka supplement (the 'Rudram' / 'Ṛgvidhāna'-like 'Rudrāṣṭnama'). It is a long, intricate praise in the form of a dialogue (the 'namo' invocations), expanding from the first aṇu-verse ('namo ... Rudrāya') through progressive rounds (the 11 and 111 repetitions of the namo), culminating in the famed 'Nīlamegha' (dark-cloud) description. It is the chief text recited in the Rudra-abhiseka / Chāturmāsa rites, and the Rudra-adhyāya is counted as one of the three 'mahā-adhyāyas' of the Yajurveda.

title: Śākta Tantras
description: The Śākta Tantras: the Mahānirvāṇa Tantra, Kulārṇava Tantra, Rudrayāmala, Brahmayāmala, and the Śrīvidyā tradition (Tripurā Rahasya, Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava); their doctrine of the Goddess as supreme (Śakti/Devī), the śrīcakra, the ten Mahāvidyās, and the kuṇḍalinī yoga.

title: Sāmaveda Śākhās
description: The recensions (śākhās) of the Sāmaveda: Kauthuma (the principal surviving recension), Rāṇāyanīya, and Jaiminīya/Talavakāra.

title: Saṃsāra
description: Saṃsāra (संसार) is the cyclic process of birth, death, and rebirth, the condition of embodied existence (saṃ+√sṝ) driven by karma and the subtle body (liṅga), the soteriological 'background' of all Indian traditions. Its defining marks are impermanence (anitya), suffering (duḥkha), and non-self (anattā) in Buddhism; the three guṇas (sattva, rajas, tamas) in Sāṃkhya-Yoga; and the 'wheel' (cakra) of becoming in the Buddhist dharmacakra. Liberation (mokṣa/nirvāṇa) is the 'blowing out' (nirodha) of this wandering.

title: Saṃskāra Types
description: The sixteen principal saṃskāras (sacraments) in Dharmaśāstra: garbhādhāna (conception), puṃsavana (ensuring male offspring), sīmantonnayana (parting hair), jātakarma (birth), nāmakaraṇa (naming), niṣkramaṇa (first outing), annaprāśana (first solid food), cūḍākaraṇa (tonsure), upanayana (sacred thread), vedārambha (Vedic study), keśānta (first shaving), samāvartana (completion of studies), vivāha (marriage), and antyeṣṭi (funeral).

title: Sāṃkhya Evolution (Parinama)
description: The Sāṃkhya theory of cosmic evolution (pariṇāma) from prakṛti: the sequential manifestation of mahat (buddhi), ahaṃkāra (ego), the five tanmātras (subtle elements), the five mahābhūtas (gross elements), the five jñānendriyas (sense organs), the five karmendriyas (action organs), and manas (mind).

title: Sāṃkhya Guṇatraya
description: The three guṇas (sattva, rajas, tamas) as the constituent strands of prakṛti in Sāṃkhya philosophy.

title: Sāṃkhya Puruṣa-Prakṛti
description: The Sāṃkhya dualism of puruṣa (pure consciousness, plural, passive witness) and prakṛti (primordial matter, singular, active, composed of three guṇas).

title: Sāṃkhya Tattvas
description: The Sāṃkhya enumeration of twenty-five tattvas (principles): prakṛti (primordial matter), mahat (buddhi), ahaṃkāra, five tanmātras, five mahābhūtas, five jñānendriyas, five karmendriyas, manas, and puruṣa (consciousness).

title: Saṃnyāsa
description: Saṃnyāsa (संन्यास) is the fourth āśrama, the renunciation of worldly life and the renunciation of the fruits of action, the culmination of the fourfold social-spiritual scheme. The Gītā (18.48–56) distinguishes vānaprastha-saṃnyāsa and parivrrajja-saṃnyāsa, the latter as the mendicant path of the Ādi Śaṅkarācārya's paramparā. The Buddhist Pāramitā texts and the Jain Ācārāṅga treat saṃnyāsa as abandonment of all worldly ties. It is preceded by the qualifications (sādhana) of vairāgya, śānti, upāya, and the firm conviction (niścaya) of the identity (or non-identity) of self and ultimate reality.

title: Saptarṣi
description: The Saptarṣi (seven sages): the seven primordial sages (Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Vasiṣṭha) who are the mind-born sons of Brahmā, the authors of Vedic hymns, and the progenitors of gotras.

title: Sarasvatī Forms
description: The forms of Sarasvatī: Vāc (speech), Bhāratī (eloquence), Śāradā (autumn goddess), and Vāṇī (voice).

title: Sarasvatī
description: Sarasvatī (सरस्वती) is the Vedic goddess of speech (Vāc), learning (vidyā), music (saṃgīta), and the arts, the patron of students. The Sarasvatī-vandanā opens the study of the Vedas and the performing arts in the sandhyā ritual. The Sarasvatī-purāṇa recounts her birth from the ocean-churning. She is depicted as white-robed (śukla), holding the vīṇā, the book (pustaka), and the swan (hamsa) — the symbol of discriminative wisdom (viveka). She is honoured especially by students and artists.

title: Śaunaka Śākhā
description: The Śaunaka Śākhā is the principal surviving recension of the Atharvaveda; its texts include the Atharvaveda Saṃhitā, Gopatha Brāhmaṇa, and several Upaniṣads.

title: Śaiva Āgamas
description: The twenty-eight principal Śaiva Āgamas (e.g., Kāmika, Kāraṇa, Suprabheda, Raurava, Mṛgendra, Sarvokta, Pārameśvara, Kiraṇa, Vātula, Parameśvara) and their upāgamas; their fourfold structure (jñāna, yoga, kriyā, caryā), their doctrine of Śiva-Śakti, the pāśa (bondage) and mokṣa.

title: Śikṣā
description: Śikṣā is the Vedāṅga of phonetics and phonology, the science of correct pronunciation (uccāraṇa) and the accents (udātta, anudātta, svarita) essential for valid Vedic recitation. Its texts (the Prātiśākha works attached to each Vedic school) enumerate the fourteenfold (or twentyfold) elements of articulation (varga) and the rules of sandhi, as well as the musical modes (svara) into which the recitation is cast. Distinct recitation lineages (jaṭā, ghana, dhaḍhi, etc.) preserve the phonetic structure; the śikṣā corpus grounds the entire hermeneutic tradition's fidelity to the sonic (śabda) dimension of the Veda.

title: Śilpa Śāstra
description: The traditional Indian system of iconography and sculpture, prescribing proportions, gestures, attributes, and materials for deity images.

title: Śrāddha Types
description: The types of śrāddha (ancestral rites) in Dharmaśāstra: nitya (daily), naimittika (occasional), kāmya (desire-motivated), and the specific rites like sapiṇḍīkaraṇa, saparvaṇa, ekodiṣṭa.

title: Śruti
description: Śruti (that which is heard): the authoritative revealed texts of Hinduism, comprising the four Vedas (Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, Atharva) and their associated Brāhmaṇas, Āraṇyakas, and Upaniṣads; distinguished from Smṛti (remembered tradition).

title: Śuddhādvaita Puṣṭi
description: In Śuddhādvaita Vedānta (Vallabha), puṣṭi (grace) is the unmerited divine favor that enables the soul's participation in Kṛṣṇa's līlā.

title: Siglum
description: A siglum (abbreviated witness identifier) is a symbolic label used in a critical apparatus to designate a manuscript or edition (e.g. V for the Vulgate, Gk for a Greek Gospel manuscript, or 'M' for the Mackenzie manuscript of a Sanskrit work). Modern critical editions follow conventions (CMG, LLA) assigning unique sigla and grouping witnesses into text-families (recensions) so that the apparatus records, with each lemma, the witnesses supporting every attested variant. The Digital Critical Edition Consortium (DCEC) is extending siglum schemes to digital corpora.

title: Sītā
description: Sītā (सीता), born of the earth (Bhūmi), is the wife of Rāma and the archetype of conjugal fidelity (pativrata) in the Vālmiki Rāmāyaṇa. Raised by Janaka, she accompanies Rāma into exile and is abducted by Ravana. The fire-test (āgni-prarohaṇa) and the later forest exile and agni-cleansing test the bounds of trust. Her birth-story and her final return to the earth close the epic's treatment of dharma and the feminine principle (stri-dharma).

title: Smṛti
description: Smṛti (that which is remembered): the body of post-Vedic authoritative texts including the Dharmaśāstras (Manusmṛti, Yājñavalkyasmṛti), the Itihāsas (Mahābhārata, Rāmāyaṇa), the Purāṇas, the Āgamas, and the Vedāṅgas; distinguished from Śruti (revealed) as being of human authorship but traditionally authoritative.

title: Śrīmad Bhāgavata Commentary Traditions
description: The Bhāgavata Purāṇa (Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam) has attracted a major commentarial tradition: Śrīdhara Svāmī (14th c., Bhāvārthadīpikā Bhāṣya), Śaṅkara-deva, and the Vaiṣṇṇava exegetes Jīva Gosvāmī (Sat-khyā-tīdyā), Viśvanātha Cakravartī (Śrīmad-Bhāgavatamṛta, 1705), and Radhāmohan Gosvāmī. Their commentaries defend the Bhāgavata's primacy (muktāṅga-tantra) and reconcile its myths with Vedānta; Sat-sandarbhas and the Gopāla-campūṣaṇa are accessory. The critical edition (BORI/VA) and the Motilal Banarsidass edition supply the text for modern study.

title: Stemmatics
description: The method of reconstructing manuscript genealogies (stemma codicum) to infer textual relationships.

title: Strīdharmā
description: Strī-dharma (stri-dharma, 'the law/duty of women') is the Dharmaśāstra corpus governing the status and rites of women: the girl-child (kumārī), the maiden (virgin), the wife (patnī), and the widow (vidhava). The Dharma-sūtras and Smṛtis (Manu 5-6, Yājñavalkya 4.95) prescribe the 'three lifetimes' (triguṇa) of a woman's dharma — mītā (moderation), svādhyāya (self-study), and saṃgama (union). Modern scholarship distinguishes these textual prescriptions from the diverse regional and historical actual practice (vyavahāra) of living women.

title: Sūrya Navagraha
description: The Navagraha ('nine planets' / 'nine celestial influencers') are the group of celestial bodies whose motion governs human affairs (karmānukūla) in traditional Vedic astrology (Jyotiṣa). The nine are: Sūrya (Sun), Candra (Moon), Mangala (Mars), Budha (Mercury), Guru (Jupiter), Śukra (Venus), Śanai (Saturn), plus the shadow-lords Rāhu and Ketu (the lunar nodes). Sūrya is placed first among them as the visible 'source of light'. The Navagraha are worshipped together in homa and temple shrines (often a single 'Navagraha' shrine) and the term also names a category of temple reliefs and devotional texts (Navagraha-kāvya / Naṭa-rājāya).

title: Taittirīya Śākhā
description: The Taittirīya Śākhā is the principal surviving recension of the Kṛṣṇa (Black) Yajurveda, prevalent in South India; its texts include the Taittirīya Saṃhitā, Brāhmaṇa, Āraṇyaka, and Upaniṣad.

title: Tantra Śāstra
description: The Tantra Śāstra corpus: the textual tradition of Tantra (Śākta, Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Buddhist), characterized by ritual (kriyā), meditation (yoga), mantra, yantra, maṇḍala, and the guru-śiṣya transmission.

title: Tantra
description: Tantra: the esoteric ritual and yogic tradition transmitted through guru-śiṣya lineages, characterized by the use of mantra, yantra, maṇḍala, dīkṣā (initiation), and the worship of deities in their fierce and benign forms.

title: Textual Criticism
description: The discipline of evaluating manuscript variants to reconstruct a text's history and establish an edited text.

title: Thumri and Dadra
description: The light classical forms of Hindustani music: thumrī (romantic, erotic, based on Braj/Hindi poetry, set to dīpacandī/punjabi tāl), dadra (lighter, faster, in dadra tāl), kājrī, caitī, horī.

title: Tīrtha Types
description: The classification of tīrtha (pilgrimage sites) in Purāṇic and Dharmaśāstra tradition: deva-tīrtha (deity-associated), ṛṣi-tīrtha (sage-associated), mṛtyu-tīrtha (death-related), and the distinction between mukti-tīrtha (liberation-granting) and bhukti-tīrtha (enjoyment-granting).

title: Trisandhyā
description: The trisandhyā (three daily junctions): the Vedic prescription for worship at dawn (prātaḥ-sandhyā), noon (mādhyāhnika), and dusk (sāyaṃ-sandhyā); the Gāyatrī mantra recitation, prāṇāyāma, arghya offering, and upasthāna.

title: Vairāgya
description: Vairāgya (वैराग्य) is dispassion or detachment from sense-objects and worldly fruits, the preliminary qualification (sādhana) for the knowledge-life of Advaita and the threshold of renunciation. Śaṅkara's Vivekacandrikā distinguishes vairāgya as the wish to abandon sense-enjoyment for the Supreme. The Gītā (2.64–66) pairs vairāgya with ārjava (straightforwardness) as a twin means to mokṣa. Traditional texts distinguish śuddha vairāgya (in monks) from sāmānya (householder detachment in action). It is cultivated through the memory of death (maranasaṁsmṛti), impermanence-reflection (anitya-vihāra), and satsaṅga.

title: Vaiśeṣika Atomism
description: The Vaiśeṣika atomic theory positing four kinds of eternal, indivisible atoms (paramāṇu) — earth, water, fire, air — each with distinct qualities (guṇa); their binary combinations (dvyanuka) and ternary combinations (tryanuka) forming the gross physical world.

title: Vaiśeṣika Creation Theory
description: The Vaiśeṣika theory of creation (sṛṣṭi) and dissolution (pralaya) through the combination and separation of eternal atoms (paramāṇu) guided by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) of individual selves.

title: Vaiśeṣika Padārthas
description: The Vaiśeṣika school enumerates seven padārthas (categories of existence): dravya (substance), guṇa (quality), karma (action), sāmānya (generality), viśeṣa (particularity), samavāya (inherence), and abhāva (absence).

title: Vaiśeṣika Paramāṇu
description: The Vaiśeṣika atomic theory (paramāṇu-vāda) positing eternal, indivisible atoms as the ultimate constituents of physical substances.

title: Vaiṣṇava Āgamas
description: The Vaiṣṇava Āgamas: the Pāñcarātra corpus (e.g., Jayākhya, Ahirbudhnya, Paushkara, Sāttvata) and the Vaikhānasa texts.

title: Varṇa-āśrama Dharma
description: The integrated system of varṇa (four social classes) and āśrama (four life stages) duties in Dharmaśāstra.

title: Varṇa
description: Varṇa (वर्ण) is the traditional fourfold division of society — Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, Śūdra — rooted in the Ṛg Vedic Puruṣa Sūkta and elaborated in the Dharmaśāstras and the Jātaka stories. Varṇa is classically distinguished from jāti (birth-community), which multiplied far beyond the fourfold scheme; the Buddhist critique of varṇa as a basis for social hierarchy is found in the Aṅguttaranikāya. In the Gītā (4.13) the Lord declares varṇaṃ ... guṇaiḥ — the fourfold order as a functional taxonomy of gunas, not a rigid birth-ascriptive hierarchy. Modern scholarship treats varṇa as an idealized model rather than historical reality.

title: Vāstu Śāstra
description: The traditional Indian system of architecture and spatial design, governing temple, palace, and domestic construction.

title: Vedic Cosmology
description: Vedic cosmology: the Ṛgvedic vision of the universe (brahmāṇḍa) emerging from the cosmic sacrifice (puruṣa-sūkta, RV 10.90), the three worlds (bhūr, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ), the cosmic mountain (Meru), the seven dvīpas and oceans; the Upaniṣadic evolution to brahman as the substrate of all.

title: Vedic Deities
description: The principal Vedic deities: Agni (fire), Indra (rain/warrior), Varuṇa (cosmic order), Mitra (contracts), the Aśvins (healing), Sūrya/Savitṛ (sun), Uṣas (dawn), Vāyu (wind), Rudra (storm), Viṣṇu (strides), Pūṣan (paths), Bṛhaspati (priesthood).

title: Vedic Mantra Classification
description: The classification of Vedic mantras: ṛc (Ṛgveda verses), yajus (Yajurveda prose), sāman (Sāmaveda chants), nigada (loud recitation); the division into mantra and brāhmaṇa portions; the gāyatrī, uṣṇik, anuṣṭubh, bṛhatī, paṅkti, triṣṭubh, jagatī metres.

title: Vedic Metre (Chandas)
description: The system of Vedic metres (chandas): gāyatrī (24 syllables), uṣṇik (28), anuṣṭubh (32), bṛhatī (36), paṅkti (40), triṣṭubh (44), jagatī (48), and their use in the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā.

title: Vedic Priesthood (Ṛtvij)
description: The four principal Vedic priests (ṛtvij) and their assistants: hotṛ (Ṛgveda recitation), adhvaryu (Yajurveda ritual action), udgātṛ (Sāmaveda chanting), brahman (Atharvaveda supervision).

title: Vedic Ritual (Yajña)
description: The Vedic sacrificial system (yajña): the seven havir-yajñas (Agnihotra, Darśa-pūrṇamāsa, Āgrayaṇa, Cāturmāsya, Nirūḍhapaśubandha, Sautrāmaṇi, Agniṣṭoma) and the seven soma-yajñas (Agnistoma, Atyagniṣṭoma, Ukthya, Ṣoḍaśī, Vājapeya, Atirātra, Aptoryāma).

title: Vedic Time Cycles
description: Vedic and post-Vedic time cycles: the four yugas (Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, Kali) and their durations (4:3:2:1), the mahāyuga (4.32 million years), the manvantara (71 mahāyugas), the kalpa (1000 mahāyugas = 4.32 billion years), Brahmā's day and night.

title: Videhamukti
description: Videhamukti (वैदेहमुक्ति, 'liberation in the body-less') is liberation after death — the 'great' (parama) release that occurs when the body falls — as distinct from jīvanmukti (liberation while living). The term 'Videha' (the 'body-less one') denotes the liberated who, freed of the body (deha) and the cycle (saṃsāra), enters the 'pure' (kevala) state. The Advaita distinguishes this 'highest word' (parama-śabda) from the empirical (vyavahārika); the Gītā (8.15–16) describes the 'liberated' who return as the light (jyoti) of the supreme.

title: Vidura
description: Vidura (विदुर) is the wise elder and advisor of the Kuru court, the son of the servant and sage Dharu, whose counsel guides Yudhiṣṭhira and the state through the moral crises of the Mahābhārata. The Vidura Smṛti (Vidurasmṛti) and the Draupadi-sabha preserve his precepts on statecraft (rājanītikathā) and the duties of rulers (rājadharma). His voice of moderation and his birth transcending jāti make him the exemplar of the wise minister (amātya) whose virtue exceeds birth.

title: Viśiṣṭādvaita Nitya-vibhūti
description: In Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta, nitya-vibhūti (eternal manifestation) is the spiritual realm of Vaikuṇṭha, distinct from the material world (līlā-vibhūti).

title: Viśiṣṭādvaita Prapatti
description: In Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta, prapatti (śaraṇāgati) is the act of complete self-surrender to Viṣṇu as the sole means to liberation.

title: Viṣṇu Sahasranāma
description: The Viṣṇu Sahasranāma (thousand names of Viṣṇu) from the Mahābhārata (Anuśāsana Parva), recited by Bhīṣma to Yudhiṣṭhira.

title: Vivartavāda
description: Vivarta-vāda — the theory of apparent transformation — is Advaita Vedānta's doctrine that the world is an illusory appearance (vivarta) superimposed on Brahman, not a real change. Śaṅkara argues in the Brahma-sūtra Bhāṣya (1.4.2) that since Brahman is immutable, the manifold cannot be a real transformation; the rope-snake (adhyāsa) illustrates perception imposing form on formless. The doctrine is defended against Buddhist idealism and the Sāṃkhya realism; it grounds Advaita's epistemic hierarchy (śruti over anumāna and pratyakṣa in matters of ultimate reality).

title: Vrata Categories
description: The classification of vrata (vows/observances) in Smṛti and Purāṇic tradition: nitya (daily), naimittika (occasion-specific), kāmya (desire-motivated), the upavāsa (fasting) types, the kāla-vratas (time-based), and the kāyika-vācika-mānasa distinction.

title: Vrata Dharma
description: The role of vrata (vowed observance) in Dharmaśāstra: the classification into nitya (daily), naimittika (occasion-specific), and kāmya (desire-motivated); the components of vrata (saṅkalpa, upavāsa, japa, dāna, pūjā).

title: Vyākaraṇa
description: Vyākarakṣa (grammar) is the Vedāṅga of linguistic analysis, systematized by Pāṇini in the Aṣṭādhyāyī (c. 4th c. BCE) in 399 sutras with the A bhikṣuṇī and Śiva sutras. Its economy (samāsa, sandhi) defines the phonological operations (ādeśa, āgama, parasa) and the derivational morphology (kāraka, karma, kriya) that secure correct recitation and interpretation of the Vedas and the literature. The Mahābhāṣya of Patañjali defends the grammar against Mīmāṃsā exegesis and Buddhist critiques; the tradition of commentaries (Kātyāyana, Pūjyayi) remained the locus of Indian linguistic theory until modern times.

title: Vyavahāra
description: The Dharmaśāstra category of vyavahāra (legal procedure): the courts, evidence (pramāṇa), types of disputes (vivāda), punishments (daṇḍa), and the procedural rules for litigation.

title: Yajña Types
description: The classification of yajña in Vedic and Smṛta tradition: nitya (daily, like agnihotra), naimittika (occasional), kāmya (desire-motivated), the seven havir-yajñas, the seven soma-yajñas, and the mahāyajñas (panca-mahāyajña).

title: Yajurveda Śākhās
description: The recensions (śākhās) of the Yajurveda: Kṛṣṇa (Black) Yajurveda śākhās — Taittirīya, Maitrāyaṇīya, Kaṭha, Kāpiṣṭhala — and Śukla (White) Yajurveda śākhās — Mādhyandina and Kāṇva.

title: Yoga Aṣṭāṅga
description: The eight limbs (aṣṭāṅga) of Patañjali's Yoga: yama (restraints), niyama (observances), āsana (posture), prāṇāyāma (breath control), pratyāhāra (sense withdrawal), dhāraṇā (concentration), dhyāna (meditation), samādhi (absorption).

title: Yoga Kleśas
description: The five kleśas (afflictions) in Patañjali's Yoga: avidyā (ignorance), asmitā (egoism), rāga (attachment), dveṣa (aversion), abhiniveśa (fear of death).

title: Yoga Nidrā
