description: Yoga Nidrā (yogic sleep): a guided relaxation and meditation technique leading to a state of conscious deep sleep between waking and sleeping.

title: Yoga Samādhi
description: The Yoga concept of samādhi (absorption): the stages of saṃprajñāta (with cognitive content — vitarka, vicāra, ānanda, asmitā) and asaṃprajñāta (without cognitive content, nirbīja).

title: Yoga Samāpatti
description: The state of samāpatti (coalescence) in Patañjali's Yoga, where the mind becomes transparent like a crystal reflecting the object of meditation.

title: Yoga Viveka-khyāti
description: The Yoga concept of viveka-khyāti (discriminative knowledge) as the direct intuitive realization of the distinction between puruṣa (consciousness) and prakṛti (matter); its attainment through the practice of the eight limbs (aṣṭāṅga) leading to kaivalya (liberation).

title: Yoga
description: Yoga (योग) is the discipline (yuj, 'to yoke') of the self (ātman) for the cessation of the mind's modifications (citta-vṛtti-nirodha). The Yoga of Patañjali (Yoga-sūtras) is the 'eight-limbed' (ashtanga): yama, niyama, āsana, prāṇāyāma, pratyāhāra, dhāraṇā, dhyāna, samādhi. The Gītā teaches the 'three' (tripartite) yoga — karma (action), jñāna (knowledge), and bhakti (devotion) — as convergent (samanvaya) means to the one goal (para). Yoga is both the theory (śāstra) and the practice (abhyāsa) of the self's purification and union.

title: Yudhiṣṭhira
description: Yudhiṣṭhira (युधिष्ठिर) the 'firm-in-battle', eldest of the Pāṇḍavas (son of Dharma), is the 'righteous king' (dharma-rāja) whose truthfulness earned him the epithet 'the truthful one'. He plays the fatal dice (dyūta) and loses the kingdom, wife, and brothers — the cause of the war. The Mahābhārata (Vana and Śānti Parvas) records his counsel and the 'test' (parikṣā) of his virtue; after the war he ascends the throne and rules the 'age of truth' (satya-yuga), the father of the new lineage.

title: Āyurveda
description: Āyurveda (आयुर्वेद) is the traditional Indian science of life ('life-knowledge'), codified in the Suśruta-saṃhitā (surgery, the 'sharp' bheṣaja) and the Caraka-saṃhitā (medicine), with Vāgbhaṭa's Aṣṭāṅga-saṅgraha. Its foundation is the tridoṣa theory (vāta, pitta, kapha): health (svasthya) is balance of the doṣas with digestive fire (agni) and the seven dhātu; the 'five' great elements (mahābhūta) underlie form. It prescribes āhāra (diet), vihāra (lifestyle) and seasonal (ṛtu) treatments, and classifies the three constitutional types (doṣa-prakṛti).

title: Bhārata Nāṭyam
description: The classical dance form of Tamil Nadu, reconstructed in the 20th century from sadir traditions.

title: Bidriware
description: Bidriware, the metal handicraft of Bidar (Karnataka), characterized by silver inlay on a blackened zinc-copper alloy; its Persian origins (14th century), motifs (floral, geometric, calligraphic), and products (vases, boxes, jewelry).

title: Karnāṭaka Saṅgīta
description: Karnāṭaka Saṅgīta (कर्नाटक संगीत / கர்நாடக சங்கீதம் / കർണാടക സംഗീതం), the classical music tradition of South India (Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana). Core: rāga (melodic framework), tāḷa (rhythmic cycle), and compositional forms — varṇam, kṛti, tillāṇa, javali, padam, svarajati. The Trinity (18th-19th c.): Tyāgarāja (kṛti perfection, bhakti), Muttusvāmi Dīkṣitar (Sanskrit, śrī vidyā, western notes), Śyāma Śāstri (Svarajati, Kāmākṣi). Pedagogy: sarali varisai, jaṇṭai varisai, daṭṭu varisai, alankāram, gītaṃ, svarajati, varṇam, kṛti. The 72 melakarta rāga system (Venkatamakhin). Instruments: vīṇā, veṇu, violin, mṛdaṅgam, ghaṭam, kanjira, morsing. The December Music Season (Chennai) is the world's largest classical music festival.

title: Citrakalā
description: Chitrakalā (चित्रकला, 'the art of painting') is the Indian pictorial tradition, from fresco murals (the Buddhist caves of Ajanta and Bagh, the temples of Orissa and Tamil Nadu) and court miniatures (Mughal, Rajput, Pahari, Deccani) to folk and tribal styles (Madhubani, Warli, Gond, Patachitra). Painting is counted among the sixty-four kalās and is grounded in the rasa (aesthetic sentiment) and bhāva (emotion) theory of the Nāṭya-śāstra, linking it to the poetics (kāvya) and the iconography (mūrti) of Hindu and Buddhist art.

title: Dhanurveda
description: Dhanurveda (धनुर्वेद) is the 'bow-Veda,' an Upaveda of the Yajur Veda treating archery and arms as the martial lore of the kṣatriyas. It covers the bow and arrow (dhana-bāṇa), the sword (khadga), the spear (śakti), and the theory of the bow's constituents (wood, fiber, sinew). It is cited in the Mahābhārata's war passages as the astra-śāstra (weapon-science) and underlies the later gadā-yuddha (mace-fighting) and mallayuddha (wrestling) traditions.

title: Dokra Art
description: The Dokra (Dhokra) non-ferrous metal casting tradition of the tribal communities of Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, and Odisha; the lost-wax casting technique (cire perdue) creating brass/bronze figurines of deities, animals, and daily life.

title: Gāndharva Veda
description: The Gandharva Veda (गान्धर्ववेद) is the music (saṃgīta) Upaveda of the Sāma Veda, the theoretical-and-practical foundation of Indian classical music. The 'celestial musicians' (gandharvas) are the source of the rāga (melodic mode) and the tāla (rhythmic cycle) and of song-and-dance (gīta-nṛtya). The Gandharva system of the svaras (sa-re-ga-ma-pa-da-ni) and the seven melodic types (mūḍha) form the basis of the sargam system and the later mārga and deśī traditions.

title: Hindustānī Saṅgīta
description: The classical music tradition of North India, with its rāga, tāḷa, and forms (dhrupad, khayāl, ṭhumrī).

title: Kalamkari Painting
description: The Kalamkari (pen-craft) painting tradition of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana (Srikalahasti and Machilipatnam styles); hand-painted or block-printed cotton textiles with natural dyes depicting Rāmāyaṇa, Mahābhārata, and Purāṇic themes.

title: Kāṭhakaḷi
description: Kāṭhakaḷi (കഥകളി), Kerala's classical dance-drama (17th century synthesis of Kṛṣṇanāṭṭam, Rāmanāṭṭam, and folk traditions). Key elements: elaborate vesham (makeup/costume) — paccā (green, noble), kaṭṭi (knife, anti-hero), kari (black, demoness), taṭi (beard: white=divine, red=evil, black=hunter), minukku (radiant, female/sage); the navarasas (nine emotions) through facial muscles (netrābhinaya); the āṭṭakathās (scripts) from Mahābhārata, Rāmāyaṇa, Bhāgavata (e.g., Nalacaritam, Kalyāṇasaugandhikam); sopāna-saṅgīta (Sopana music) with ceṇḍa, maṭalam, elathāḷam; rigorous gurukula training (8-10 years) at Kala Mandalam, Kottakkal. Recognized by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage. A synthesis of nṛtya (dance), nṛtta (pure movement), and nāṭya (drama).

title: Kucipuḍi
description: Kuchipudi is a classical dance-drama of Andhra Pradesh performed by the village actor-dancer-singer in an all-in-one theatrical style. Its signature items are the Tarangam (a balanced dance on a plate of milk and flowers), the 'Jatra' story-scenes, and the dance (nṛtya) of the Krishna-legend. One of the eight classical dance forms, it is celebrated for its rhythmic footwork (tāḷa) and the vivid abhinaya (expression) of the story (kathā).

title: Madhubani Painting
description: The Madhubani (Mithila) painting tradition of Bihar, characterized by geometric patterns, natural dyes, and ritual themes.

title: Manipuri
description: The classical dance tradition of Manipur, with its devotional themes (Rāsa Līlā), subtle movements, and distinctive costume.

title: Meenakari
description: Meenakari (enamelling), the art of decorating metal surfaces (gold, silver, copper) with colored enamel; its Persian origins, centers in Jaipur, Udaipur, Delhi, and Varanasi; its application on jewelry, weapons, and decorative objects.

title: Mohiniyāṭṭam
description: Mohiniyāṭṭam (മോഹിനിയാട്ടം), Kerala's classical solo dance (lasya style), traditionally performed by women. Reconstructed in the 1930s by V.N. Menon and Kala Mandalam (Vallathol Narayana Menon, Mukundraj). Key elements: graceful circular movements (cuzhippu), swaying gait (gamana), subtle facial expressions (sāttvika abhinaya), white/cream costume with gold border (kasavu), jasmine hair adornment. The repertoire: colkeṭṭu (invocation), jati-svaram, varṇam, padam, tillānā. Music: Sopana style, Carnatic rāgas (Tōḍi, Bhairavi, Kalyāṇi), accompaniment: veena, veṇu, maddaḷam, eḷattāḷam. Themes: Śṛṅgāra (love), Bhakti (devotion to Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa). Mohinī = Viṣṇu's enchantress form (distributing amṛta). Recognized by Sangeet Natak Akademi.

title: Oḍissī
description: The Odissi is a classical dance of India's eastern coast, a ritual and narrative dance of the body (kāya-nṛtya) distinguished by the tribhanga (three-bend) posture, the torso-arch (ḍolā) and the side-arm (paṭāka). It is associated with the Jagannātha and the Sūrya traditions — the temple-dance (maṇḍapa) of Puri and the dance-sculptures of the Sun Temple at Konark. Revived in the 20th century by Kelucharan Mohapatra, it is one of the eight classical dance forms, noted for its lyrical (lāsyātana) abhinaya.

title: Pahari Miniature Painting
description: The Pahari miniature painting schools of the Himalayan foothills: Basohli (bold colors, geometric), Kangra (lyrical, naturalistic), Guler, Chamba, Mandi, Kullu, and Jammu.

title: Pattachitra Painting
description: The Pattachitra cloth painting tradition of Odisha and West Bengal, characterized by bold lines, natural colors, and themes from Jagannātha cult, Rāmāyaṇa, and Mahābhārata.

title: Pichwai Painting
description: The Pichwai painting tradition of Nathdwara (Rajasthan), large cloth paintings hung behind the Śrīnāthajī deity (Kṛṣṇa as seven-year-old).

title: Rajasthani Miniature Painting
description: The Rajasthani miniature painting schools: Mewar (Udaipur), Marwar (Jodhpur), Bundi, Kota, Kishangarh, Jaipur, and Bikaner.

title: Saṃskṛta Nāṭya
description: The classical Sanskrit theatre tradition, with its nāṭyaśāstra foundation, dramatic types (nāṭaka, prakaraṇa), and playwrights (Kālidāsa, Bhāsa, Śūdraka, Bhavabhūti).

title: Thanjavur Painting
description: The Thanjavur (Tanjore) painting tradition of Tamil Nadu, characterized by gold leaf, vibrant colors, and gesso work.

title: Warli Painting
description: The Warli painting tradition of the Warli tribe (Maharashtra–Gujarat border), characterized by white geometric figures on mud walls depicting daily life, nature, and rituals.

title: Ayyappan
description: Ayyappan (അയ്യപ്പന്‍ / ஐயப்பன்), also Śāstā, Hariharaputra, Dharma-Śāstā — the deity of Sabarimala, born from the union of Śiva and Viṣṇu (as Mohinī). Embodies the synthesis of Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava traditions. Key attributes: celibacy (naiṣṭhika brahmacarya), the 18 holy steps (paṭinēṭṭāmpaṭi / பதினெட்டாம்படி), the 41-day vrata (maṇḍala kālam / மண்டல காலம்) with strict observances (black/blue clothes, no shaving, brahmacarya, daily bath). The pilgrimage to Sabarimala (Kerala) draws 40-50 million annually (Nov-Jan). The Makaravilakku (Makara Jyoti) on Makara Saṅkrānti is the climax. Worshipped across Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, and beyond. The Vāvaru (Muslim devotee) shrine at Erumeli exemplifies communal harmony. ---

title: Devī
description: Devī (देवी / தேவி / ਦੇਵੀ / ദേവি / দেবী), the Goddess, Śakti, Ambikā, Durgā, Pārvatī, Kālī, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Mahiṣāsuramardinī, Caṇḍikā, Annapūrṇā, Kāmākṣī, Mīnākṣī. Central to Śākta traditions (Śrīvidyā, Kālikā, Durgā Pūjā). The Devī Māhātmya (Durgā Saptashatī, Caṇḍī-pāṭha) is the foundational text. Manifestations: Navadurgā (9 forms), Daśamahāvidyā (10 wisdom goddesses), Aṣṭalakṣmī (8 Lakṣmīs). Consort of Śiva (Pārvatī), Viṣṇu (Lakṣmī), Brahmā (Sarasvatī). Festivals: Navarātrī/Durgā Pūjā, Vasanta Navarātrī, Kālī Pūjā, Lakṣmī Pūjā, Sarasvatī Pūjā. Śākta Pīṭhas: 51/108 sites (Kāmākhyā, Kālikā, Jvālāmukhī, Viśālākṣī). --- The Goddess in her manifold forms; this record represents the broad category of Devī-centered traditions without collapsing their distinct textual and ritual expressions.

title: Gaṇeśa
description: Gaṇeśa (गणेश / விநாயகர் / గణేష్ / ಗಣೇಶ / ഗണപതി / গণেশ / ગણેશ), Vināyaka, Piḷḷaiyār, Vighneśvara, Gajānanā — the elephant-headed deity, remover of obstacles (Vighnahartā), lord of beginnings. Son of Śiva and Pārvatī. Consorts: Siddhi (success), Buddhi (wisdom); or Ṛddhi/Siddhi. Vehicle: Mūṣaka (mouse). Attributes: broken tusk (ekadanta), modaka (sweet), axe, noose. Key texts: Gaṇeśa Purāṇa, Mudgala Purāṇa, Gaṇeśa Atharvaśīrṣa. Worshipped first in all rituals. Festivals: Gaṇeśa Caturthī (Bhādrapada Śukla Caturthī), Vināyaka Caturthī, Saṅkaṣṭī Caturthī (monthly). Regional: Mumbai's Lalbaugcha Raja, Pune's Dagdusheth, Tamil Nadu's Piḷḷaiyārpatti, Kerala's Koṭṭārakkara. --- A widely revered deity whose iconography, narratives, and ritual roles vary across regions, texts, and devotional communities.

title: Narasiṃha
description: Narasiṃha, the man-lion avatar of Viṣṇu, whose emergence from the pillar to protect Prahlāda and slay Hiraṇyakaśipu is a central Vaiṣṇava narrative.

title: Pārvatī
description: Pārvatī (Umā), the consort of Śiva and the embodiment of Śakti, her forms as Durgā, Kālī, Annapūrṇā, and Gaurī.

title: Śiva
description: Śiva (शिव / சிவன் / ಶಿವ / ശിവന്‍ / শিব / શિવ), the Auspicious One, Maheśvara, Rudra, Paśupati, Nīlakaṇṭha, Naṭarāja (cosmic dancer), Dakṣiṇāmūrti (guru), Ardhanārīśvara (half-female). Central to Śaiva traditions (Śaiva Siddhānta, Kashmir Śaivism, Vīraśaivism, Liṅgāyat). The liṅga (aniconic form) is the primary worship focus. Twelve Jyotirliṅgas. Consort: Pārvatī/Śakti. Sons: Gaṇeśa, Skanda. Vāhana: Nandi (bull). Abode: Kailāsa. Key texts: Śiva Purāṇa, Liṅga Purāṇa, Śaiva Āgamas, Tirumuṟai (Tamil). Festivals: Mahāśivarātri, Pradosha, Kārttikai Tīpam. --- A major deity with diverse textual, ritual, and regional forms; this record does not impose a single theology on the many traditions that center on Śiva.

title: Skanda
description: A deity with prominent roles in Purāṇic, Tamil, and regional traditions; his narratives and epithets vary significantly across textual and geographical contexts.

title: Sūrya
description: The solar deity represented in Vedic, Puranic, and living traditions; this record distinguishes textual portrayals from later syncretic developments.

title: Viṣṇu
description: Viṣṇu (विष्णु / விஷ்ணு / ವಿಷ್ಣು / വിഷ്ണു / বিষ্ণુ / વિષ્ણು), the All-Pervading One, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, Vāsudeva, Govinda, Madhava, Keśava. Central to Vaiṣṇava traditions (Śrīvaiṣṇavism, Gauḍīya, Puṣṭimārga, Nimbārka, Madhva). Ten principal avatāras (daśāvatāra): Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Paraśurāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, Kalki. Consort: Lakṣmī/Śrī. Abode: Vaikuṇṭha. Vāhana: Garuḍa. Attributes: Śaṅkha (conch), Cakra (discus), Gada (mace), Padma (lotus). Key texts: Viṣṇu Purāṇa, Bhāgavata Purāṇa, Nārāyaṇīya, Pāñcarātra Āgamas, Nālāyira Divya Prabandham (Tamil). Festivals: Janmāṣṭamī, Rāma-navamī, Vaikuṇṭha Ekādaśī, Onam (Vāmana), Dīpāvalī. --- A major deity with diverse textual, ritual, and regional forms; this record does not impose a single theology on the many traditions that center on Viṣṇu.

title: Viṭṭhala
description: Viṭṭhala (Vithoba, Paṇḍurāṅga), the deity of Pandharpur, Maharashtra, a form of Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa standing on a brick (viṭ); the Vārkarī tradition, the annual Palkhi pilgrimage from Alandi and Dehu, the abhangas of Jñāneśvar and Tukārām.

title: Adhika Māsa
description: The intercalary lunar month inserted approximately every 32.5 months to align lunar and solar calendars; considered especially auspicious for ritual and charity.

title: Akṣaya Tṛtīyā
description: A festival falling on the third lunar day of bright Vaiśākha, associated with prosperity, new ventures, and the descent of Gaṅgā; observances vary by region and tradition.

title: Bihu
description: The Assamese festival cycle of three Bihus (Rongali, Kongali, Bhogali) aligned with agricultural seasons; Rongali Bihu in April is the most prominent.

title: Cāturmāsya
description: The four-month monsoon period (Āṣāḍha–Kārttika) when ascetics traditionally remain stationary and householders observe additional vows; its observances vary by tradition.

title: Chhath Pūjā
description: A festival dedicated to Sūrya and Chhathī Maiyā, observed primarily in Bihar, Jharkhand, and eastern Uttar Pradesh with rigorous fasting, river bathing, and sunrise/sunset offerings.

title: Deva Uthānī Ekādaśī
description: The Ekādaśī in bright Kārttika marking Viṣṇu's awakening from cosmic sleep (yoganidrā); marks the end of Cāturmāsya and resumption of auspicious activities.

title: Dīpāvalī
description: Dīpāvalī (दीपावली / தீபாவளி / ദീപാവലি / दिवाळी), the Festival of Lights (dīpa-āvalī = row of lamps). Five days: Dhanteras (wealth, Dhanvantarī), Narka Caturdashī (Kṛṣṇa slays Narakāsura), Amāvasyā (main day, Lakṣmī Pūjā, Rāma's return to Ayodhyā), Govardhan Pūjā (Kṛṣṇa lifts Govardhan), Bhāi Dooj (sibling bond). Lighting dīpas (oil lamps), rangoli, fireworks, sweets, new clothes. Regional: Kālī Pūjā (Bengal, same night), Bandi Chhor Divas (Sikh, Guru Hargobind's release), Bestu Varas (Gujarati New Year), Balipratipada (Maharashtra). Jain: Mahāvīra's nirvāṇa. The universal celebration of light over darkness, knowledge over ignorance. --- A festival of lights observed across regions and communities with varied narratives, rituals, and historical associations.

title: Vijayadaśamī / Dussehra
description: Vijayadaśamī (Dussehra), the tenth day after Navarātri, celebrating the victory of good over evil: Durgā's victory over Mahiṣāsura (East/West India) and Rāma's victory over Rāvaṇa (North India); observed with Rāmalīlā enactments, effigy burning (Rāvaṇa, Kumbhakarṇa, Meghanāda), and the worship of weapons (śastra-pūjā).

title: Gaṇeśa Caturthī
description: Gaṇeśa Caturthī, the ten-day festival celebrating Gaṇeśa's birth, observed in Bhādrapada (Aug–Sep); clay idol installation, daily pūjā, modak offerings, and immersion (visarjan) on Ananta Caturdaśī.

title: Gītā Jayantī
description: A festival commemorating the Bhagavad Gītā's revelation, observed on Mokṣadā Ekādaśī in Mārgaśīrṣa; its observances include recitation and discourse.

title: Guru Pūrṇimā
description: A festival honoring spiritual teachers, observed on the full moon of Āṣāḍha in Hindu traditions; Buddhist and Jain traditions observe related festivals on different dates; specific observances vary by lineage and region.

title: Hartālika Tīja
description: A festival observed primarily by women in North and Central India for marital well-being, associated with Pārvatī's penance for Śiva; practices vary by region.

title: Holī
description: Holī, the spring festival of colours observed on the full moon of Phālguna (Feb–Mar); the evening Holikā Dahan (bonfire) commemorating Prahlāda's survival, and the day of colour play (Raṅgavalī Holī) celebrating divine love (Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa).

title: Kṛṣṇa Janmāṣṭamī
description: Kṛṣṇa Janmāṣṭamī, the festival of Kṛṣṇa's birth, observed on the eighth day (aṣṭamī) of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada (Aug–Sep); midnight celebration of Kṛṣṇa's birth, fasting, bhajans, dahi handi (pot-breaking) in Maharashtra, Rāsa Līlā enactments in Vṛndāvana.

title: Kārttikai Deepam
description: The Tamil festival of lights on the full moon of Kārttikai (Nov–Dec), dedicated to Śiva as the infinite light.

title: Kumbha Melā
description: A massive periodic pilgrimage festival held at four sites—Prayagraj, Haridwar, Ujjain, and Nashik—on different cycles; its historical development, sectarian participation, and site-specific management are complex and varied.

title: Lohrī
description: A Punjabi winter festival marking the passing of the winter solstice, celebrated with bonfires, folk songs, and distribution of sweets; its observances are regionally specific.

title: Māgha Mela
description: The annual Māgha Mela at Prayāgraja (Allahabad), Uttar Pradesh, during the month of Māgha (Jan–Feb), a smaller precursor to the Kumbha Mela.

title: Mahāśivarātri
description: Mahāśivarātri, the 'Great Night of Śiva', observed on the 14th night of the dark fortnight of Phālguna/Māgha (Feb–Mar); all-night vigil (jāgaraṇa), fasting, Rudrābhiṣeka, bilva leaf offerings, and the chanting of 'Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya'.

title: Makara Saṅkrānti
description: The solar transition into Capricorn (Makara), marking uttarāyaṇa; celebrated across India with diverse regional names and practices (Pongal, Lohri, Magh Bihu, etc.).

title: Nāga Pañcamī
description: A festival honoring serpent deities (nāgas) on the fifth day of bright Śrāvaṇa; its observances, including milk offerings and snake imagery, vary regionally.

title: Navarātri
description: Navarātri (नवरात्रि / நவராத்திரி / നവരാത്രि / নৰরাত্রি / नवरात्री), the nine nights (nava-rātri) dedicated to the Goddess in her three guṇa-forms: Durgā (tamas, days 1-3), Lakṣmī (rajas, days 4-6), Sarasvatī (sattva, days 7-9). Autumn (Śarad, Sept-Oct) and Spring (Vasanta, Mar-Apr). Regional expressions: Durgā Pūjā (Bengal, pandals, immersion), Golu/Kolu (Tamil Nadu/Kerala, doll displays), Bathukamma (Telangana, flower stacks), Garbā/Dāṇḍiyā (Gujarat, circle dances), Mysore Dasara (royal procession), Ramlila (North, Rāma enactment), Ayudha Pūjā (tools/vehicles worship, day 9). Vijayadaśamī (day 10) = Dussehra (Rāma's victory) / Vidyarambha (initiation of learning). Fasting, devī-māhātmya recitation, kanya-pūjana (girls worshipped). ---

title: Oṇam
description: Oṇam (ഓണം), the state festival of Kerala, celebrated for ten days in the month of Ciṅgam (Aug-Sep). Commemorates the annual visit of Mahābali (Māvēli), the benevolent asura king, who was sent to Pātāla by Vāmana (Viṣṇu's dwarf avatāra) but granted a yearly return. Key elements: Pukkalam (floral rangoli), Oṇasadhya (feast on banana leaf with 20+ dishes), Vallam-kaḷi (snake boat races), Pulikkali (tiger dance), Tiruvaṭira (women's dance). The festival unites communities across religious lines. Glorified in the Nālāyira Divya Prabandham and associated with the Tṛkkākkāra Vāmana Temple. --- A Kerala festival combining harvest commemoration with the mythological narrative of Mahabali and Vamana; its practices and narratives vary across communities and are represented here with attention to regional grounding.

title: Pongal
description: A Tamil harvest festival marking the sun's northward journey (uttarāyaṇa); its four days (Bhogi, Surya, Mattu, Kaanum) feature distinct regional practices and foods.

title: Rakṣābandhana
description: Rakṣābandhana (Rakhi), the festival of the protective bond between siblings, observed on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa (Aug); the sister ties a rakhi (sacred thread) on the brother's wrist, and the brother vows protection.

title: Rāma Navamī
description: Rāma Navamī, the festival of Rāma's birth, observed on the ninth day (navamī) of the bright fortnight of Caitra (Mar–Apr); Rāma-pūjā, Rāmāyaṇa recitation, Rāmalīlā enactments, and the ceremonial wedding (Sītā-Rāma kalyāṇam) in South India.

title: Ratha Yātrā
description: The chariot festival of Jagannātha at Purī, where the deities are taken in massive chariots to Guṇḍicā Temple; its scale, rituals, and participation are distinctive to Odisha.

title: Thai Pusam
description: The Tamil festival dedicated to Skanda/Murugaṇ on the full moon of Thai (Jan–Feb), observed with kavadi (burden-bearing), piercings, and processions.

title: Ugādi
description: The New Year festival in Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, and Karnataka, marking the first day of Chaitra; observed with ritual baths, new clothes, and the Ugadi pachadi (six tastes).

title: Baisākhī
description: The Punjabi harvest festival and Sikh New Year, commemorating the Khalsa's founding in 1699; observed with processions, kirtan, and community meals (langar). ---

title: Vaṭa Sāvitrī
description: A festival observed by married women for their husbands' longevity, centered on the banyan tree (vaṭa) and the Sāvitrī-Satyavān narrative; practices vary regionally.

title: Viṣu
description: Viṣu (വിഷു), the Malayalam New Year (Kolla Varṣam), observed on the first day of Meḍam (mid-April) when the Sun enters Meṣa Rāśi. The central ritual is Viṣukkaṇi (വിഷുക്കണി) — the auspicious first sight arranged the night before: a kaṇikonna (golden shower) flowers, rice, coconut, fruits, gold coins, mirror, and the Bhagavad Gītā or Rāmāyaṇa placed before Kṛṣṇa's image. Elders give Kaiṇeṭṭam (money gifts) to younger members. The Sādya feast includes viṣu-kaṭṭu (banana chips), māṅgā-caru (mango curry), and pāyaśam. Fireworks and the Viṣu-veḷḷa (boat race) at Aranmula. Marks the agricultural new year in Kerala. --- The Malayalam New Year in Kerala, marking the sun's transit into Meda Rāśi; observed with the Vishukkani (auspicious first sight), money gifts (kaineettam), and feasting.

title: Guru
description: Guru (गुरु) is the spiritual teacher/preceptor (the dispeller of darkness), the second of the three jewels (triratna) and the conduit of the paramparā (lineage) of knowledge. The guru is honored as the 'second birth' (dwitīya-janma) and the 'eye of knowledge' (jñāna-cakṣu); the Gītā (4.38) declares jñāna greater than karma because the guru reveals the self (ātman). The guru-disciple (guru-śiṣya) relationship structures the transmission of the Vedas (gurukula), the Vedānta, and the Tantric and devotional (bhakti) lineages; the teacher is the living embodiment of the tradition (paramparā-vāṇī).

title: Mantra
description: Mantra (मन्त्र) is a sacred utterance (the 'mind-tool' = man + tra) used in invocation, protection, and transformation, the formula of the Vedic (Ṛg) and the tantric (tantric) disciplines. The Gītā (6.16–17) and the Mantra-ratnākara define its efficacy as the syllable (bīja), the name (nāma), and the formula (vyāpti), with the breath (prāṇa) and concentration (dhāraṇā). Categories include the pauruṣa (personal) and the a-puruṣa (impersonal), the dhyāna-mantra (e.g. Gāyatrī), and the kāla-mantra (e.g. Asya-vacana). A mantra's power (śakti) is believed to be activated by the guru's empowerment (dīkṣā).

title: Prasāda
description: Prasāda (प्रसाद) is the sanctified remnant of a offering (naivedya) distributed to devotees after worship (puja), the 'grace that falls' (prasāda) from the divine. The term also denotes the divine grace (śakti) that descends as food and the 'sweetness' (madhurā) of spiritual experience. The distribution of prasāda (pradakṣina and prasāda) is central to the temple and the household ritual; it is shared as an equalizing social element (no caste) and is held to carry the blessing of the deity (āśirvāda). Its preparation (e.g. coconuts, sweets) is codified.

title: Annamācārya
description: Annamācārya (1408–1503), the earliest known composer of saṅkīrtana (devotional songs) in Telugu, dedicated to Veṅkaṭeśvara of Tirumala.

title: Appayya Dīkṣita
description: Appayya Dīkṣita (1520–1593), the Advaita Vedānta scholar and Śaiva devotee, author of over 100 works including the Siddhānta-leśa-saṅgraha, Śivārkamaṇi-dīpikā, and Khaṇḍana-khaṇḍa-khādya.

title: Caitanya Mahāprabhu
description: Caitanya Mahāprabhu (1486–1534) was the 16th-century Gaudiya founder who proclaimed the supremacy of krīḍā (congregational chanting) of the names of Kṛṣṇa (nāma-saṅkīrtana) as the yuga-dharma of the Kali age. Born Viṭṭa Haricāṇḍa in Nadia (Bengal), he journeyed across the Ganga basin teaching bhakti as the path of love, and established the rukmiṇā-siddha-saṅgha (devotee community). His theology (jīva-svabhāvika and ādi-svarūpa) is recorded in the Śikṣāṣṭaka, the Caitanya-caritāmṛta (Kṛṣṇa-das Kavirāja) and the Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu (Rūpa Gosvāmī). The Gaudiya tradition (sampradāya) traces its ādi-guru lineage through him to Nityananda and Advaita Ācārya.

title: Jīva Gosvāmī
description: Jīva Gosvāmī (1616–1706) was the pre-eminent ācārya of the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava school, the principal architect of its theology, and a scholar-poet of the Vṛndāvan tradition. A disciple of the Six Gosvāmīs' followers, he composed the Sat Sandarbhas (Ṣaṭ Sandarbha) systematizing Gauḍīya doctrine — rasa theory, līlā, the six ālaṅkāras — and commentaries on the Gītā and the Bhāgavata. His kavya and the Jīva-bodhanī constitute a classical synthesis of bhakti and Sanskrit poetics; he is honoured as the bhāṣyācārya (great commentator) of the Gauḍīya line.

title: Kabīr
description: Kabīr (c. 1440–1518), the mystic poet-saint of the Bhakti movement, synthesizing Hindu and Islamic devotional traditions; his verses (bījak, sākhīs, śabdas) emphasizing nirguṇa-bhakti (devotion to the formless), the guru, and the critique of ritual orthodoxy.

title: Kanakadāsa
description: Kanakadāsa (1509–1609), the Haridāsa saint-poet from Karnataka, composer of kīrtanas in Kannada dedicated to Adikeshava (Viṣṇu); his works (Mohanatarangini, Ramadhanya Charitre, Nalacharitre) emphasizing bhakti, social equality, and devotion over caste.

title: Madhva
description: Traditional dating assigns Madhva to the 13th century CE; scholarly dates vary. He is associated with Dvaita Vedānta through traditional and textual lineages; this record represents his tradition without ranking it against other schools.

title: Muttusvāmi Dīkṣitar
description: Muttusvāmi Dīkṣitar (1775–1835), one of the Carnatic trinity, composer of ~500 kṛtis in Sanskrit, known for his mastery of rāga, the navagraha kṛtis, the kamalamba navavarṇa kṛtis, and his use of Sanskrit sahitya with intricate rāga structures.

title: Nīlakaṇṭha Dīkṣita
description: Nīlakaṇṭha Dīkṣita (1613–1697), the Advaita Vedānta scholar and poet, grandson of Appayya Dīkṣita; author of the Śiva-leśa, Śivalīlārṇava, and the satirical Kaliviḍambana.

title: Nimbārka
description: Nimbārka (c. 13th–14th c.; 'Keśava Kācyānugraha') is the 13th-century Ādi of the Nimbārka (Kumāra) sampradāya, which teaches the simultaneous oneness and difference of the soul and God (bhedābheda) — Viṣṇu and his energies (śakti) Nārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī — in a dual-aspect monism. The Nimbārka Siddha and the Nimbārka-śataka (attributed) set forth his doctrine of 'the two truths' (sat and asat) and the efficacy of the names (nāma) and surrender (prapatti). The tradition preserves the Mūlamadhyamakāla (the original work on Viśiṣṭādvaita) and a distinctive iconographic tradition of Nārāyaṇa with four arms.

title: Purandaradāsa
description: Purandaradāsa (1484–1564), the 'father of Carnatic music' (Karnataka Sangeeta Pitamaha), composer of 475,000+ kīrtanas in Kannada and Sanskrit.

title: Rāghavendra Svāmī
description: Rāghavendra Svāmī (1595–1671), the Dvaita Vedānta pontiff (Rāghavendra Maṭha, Mantralayam), known for his commentaries on Madhva's works and his reputation as a miracle-worker.

title: Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṃsa
description: Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṃsa (1836–1886), the 19th-century mystic of Dakṣiṇeśvar, devotee of Kālī, who experienced diverse religious paths (Śākta, Vaiṣṇava, Advaita, Islam, Christianity) and declared 'yato mat tato patha' (as many paths, so many ways).

title: Rāmānanda
description: Rāmānanda (c. 14th–15th century), the founder of the Rāmānandī sect, a North Indian Vaiṣṇava tradition emphasizing Rāma-bhakti and the accessibility of devotion regardless of caste; his disciples included Kabīr, Ravidās, and Sena.

title: Rāmānuja
description: Traditional dating assigns Rāmānuja to the 11th–12th century CE; scholarly dates vary. He is associated with Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta through traditional and textual lineages; this record represents his tradition without ranking it against other schools.

title: Śaṅkara
description: Traditional attribution places Śaṅkara in the 8th century CE; scholarly dating varies and historical reconstruction remains distinct from hagiographical accounts. He is associated with Advaita Vedānta through traditional and textual lineages.

title: Śyāma Śāstri
description: Śyāma Śāstri (1762–1827), one of the Carnatic trinity, composer of ~300 kṛtis in Telugu and Sanskrit, known for his swarajatis, his kamakshi navaratna mālikā, his ananda bhairavi compositions, and his distinctive rhythmic structures (tāḷa).

title: Śrī Aurobindo
description: Śrī Aurobindo (1872–1950), the nationalist, philosopher, and yogi who developed Integral Yoga (Pūrṇa Yoga).

title: Sūrdās
description: Sūrdās (c. 1478–1583), the blind poet-saint of the Puṣṭimārga (Vallabha sect), composer of the Sūrsāgar (thousands of Braj bhāṣā poems on Kṛṣṇa-līlā).

title: Tulsīdās
description: Tulsīdās (1532–1623), the composer of the Rāmacaritamānasa (Awadhi retelling of the Rāmāyaṇa), the Hanumān Cālīsā, and the Vinaya Patrikā.

title: Tyāgarāja
description: Tyāgarāja (1767–1847), one of the Carnatic trinity, composer of ~24,000 kṛtis in Telugu and Sanskrit, mostly on Rāma.

title: Vallabha
description: Vallabha (1478–1532), the Ādi of the Vallabha (Kāshapa) Sampradāya, taught Śuddhādvaita ('the sole existent is Viṣṇu, all else mithyā) and the path of kāma (divine love) through the grace of Nārāyaṇa. Regarded as a child-avatāra (bāla-avatāra), he composed the Anuvyākhyāna on the Bhāgavatam and the stutis, and established the sacred geography of Vṛndāvana. His descendants (the Puṣṭi-mārga, the 'path of nourishment' by divine grace alone) and the Vallabha-sampradāya continue in the Braj region, worshipping Nārāyaṇa with the family of divine parents (kalyāṇa-gopāla).

title: Vālmīki
description: Valmiki (or Valmika) is the traditional adikavi ('first poet') of Sanskrit literature and the ṛṣi attributed with the Rāmāyaṇa. The Vālmiki-Rāmāyaṇa (c. 24,000 ślokas) is the earliest Sanskrit epic and the source for all later Rāmāyaṇas. The Śāṇḍikas and later tradition recount his transformation from a dacoit (māṃsa) into a sage by the grace of Nārada and the Gāyatrī-mantra, making him the patron of the kāvya genre and the archetypal compiler (vyāsa) of narrative (kathā) poetry in Sanskrit.

title: Swami Vivekananda
description: Swami Vivekananda (1863–1902), the chief disciple of Rāmakṛṣṇa, the founder of the Ramakrishna Mission, the exponent of practical Vedānta at the 1893 World's Parliament of Religions (Chicago).

title: Vyāsa
description: Vyāsa (or Vyāsa-kṝṣṇa / Vedavyāsa) is the legendary ṛṣi traditionally credited with compiling the countless Vedas into the four Vedas (Samhitās, Brāhmaṇas, Aranyakas, Upaniṣads) and with the massive composition of the Mahābhārata (100,000 ślokas), which contains the Bhagavad Gītā and the Bhāgavata's principal frame. He is also the traditional author-commentator of the Brahma-sūtras (Vedānta-sūtras) and of the Harivaṃśa. As the father (pitṛ) of the kuru lineage and the pupil of the sage Dvaipāyana, he is the archetypal compiler (vyāsa) of the Hindu canon.

title: Advaita Vedānta
description: Advaita Vedānta, systematized by Ādi Śaṅkara (c. 8th c.), teaches non-duality: ātman is Brahman and all multiplicity is māyā (adhyāsa, apparent super-imposition). Its epistemology (pramāṇa) admits pratyakṣa, anumāna, and śabda (the Upaniṣads), validated by śravaṇa-manana-nididhyāsana. Śaṅkara's Brahmaphilosophy distinguishes the absolute (paramārtha) from the empirical (vyavahārika) and the apparent (prātibhāsika) levels. The tradition's commentarial lineage (bhāṣyas on the Prasthānatrayi) and its polemics with Mīmāṃsā and Buddhism shaped medieval Hindu thought; its modern exponents include the Dashāṅga and Neo-Advaita figures.

title: Nyāya
description: Nyāya, systematized by Gautama (Akṣapāda) in the Nyāya Sūtras (c. 2nd c. BCE), is the school of logical analysis and epistemology. It enumerates four pramāṇas (perception, inference, comparison, testimony) and the four pramāṇa-sādhāraṇas (sadhya, hetu, udāharaṇa, prayogika), the structure of a sound inference (vyāpti), and the sixteen categories (padārthas) culminating in the highest good (paramārtha, mokṣa). The school's logical apparatus (Hemacandra, Vātsyāyana, Ganganāthavādi) became the lingua franca of Indian philosophical debate (śāstra-saṃgrahāṇi) and influenced Vedānta, Buddhism, and Jain logic.

title: Pūrvamīmāṃsā
description: Pūrva Mīmāṃsā (Jaimini), the 'Earlier' exegesis, centres the exegesis (mīmāṃsā) of the Karmasūtras of the Vedas as the fountainhead of dharma. It holds the eternal, authorless (apauruṣeyā) Vedic injunction (śruti) and its ritual prescriptions paramount, defended through a sophisticated theory of language (abhāva-vāda, jāti) and exegesis (six āropas of Vedic interpretation). Whereas the Pūrva stresses ritual efficacy and the eternity of dharma, the Uttara (Vedānta) emphasizes jñāna. Its epistemology, grammar, and theory of scriptural authority deeply shaped Vedānta and the Dharmaśāstra tradition.

title: Sāṃkhya
description: Sāṃkhya, traditionally ascribed to Kapila, is the dualistic enumeration (siddhānta) of twenty-five tattvas from Puruṣa (consciousness) and Prakṛti (matter). Its emanation schema (Sāṃkhyakārikā of Īśvarakṛṣṇa) unfolds via the three Guṇas from the subtle avyakta through ahaṃkāra to the gross elements and the twenty-four tattvas that constitute experience. It enumerates three kinds of suffering (ādhyātmika, ādhibhautika, ādhidaivika) whose cessation (kaivalya) comes by discriminative knowledge (viveka) of Puruṣa's aloofness from Prakṛti. Yoga (Patañjali) adopts the same metaphysics and adds the practical discipline of abhyāsa-vairāgya.

title: Vaiśeṣika
description: Vaiśeṣika, systematized by Kaṇāda (c. 6th c. BCE) in the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra, is the school of atomistic pluralism (vaiśeṣika = 'difference'). It classifies reality into seven categories (padārthas): substance, quality, activity, universal, particular, inherence, and (later) non-existence, with the earth-water-fire-air-ether atoms (anu) as the material basis of the cosmos. Liberation (mokṣa) is achieved by right knowledge (pramā) of these categories and the Self's distinctness from the body. The school's later synthesis with Nyāya produced Navya-Nyāya's analytic epistemology; its atomic theory influenced later Jain and Buddhist cosmology.

title: Vedānta
description: Vedānta ('end of the Vedas') denotes the darsana grounded in the Prasthānatrayi — the Upaniṣads (primary), the Bhagavad Gītā (bridge), and the Brahma-sūtras (summary) — systematized from the 8th c. It adjudicates the nature of Brahman and its relation to the world and the self through three great epistemological stances: non-dualism (Advaita, Śaṅkara), qualified non-dualism (Viśiṣṭādvaita, Rāmānuja), and dualism (Dvaita, Madhva), later joined by Śuddhādvaita (Vallabha), Dvaitin (Nimbārka), and the Gauḍīya tradition (Jīva). Its modern history includes the Hindu Renaissance (Rāmana, Vivekananda) and contemporary Advaitic and Neo-Vedānta movements.

title: Yoga Darśana
description: Yoga (darśana) is the school systematized by Patañjali in the Yoga Sūtras (c. 2nd c. BCE–2nd c. CE), which adopts Sāṃkhya metaphysics and prescribes the eight-limbed path (ashtanga: yama, niyama, āsana, prāṇāyāma, pratyāhāra, dhāraṇā, dhyāna, samādhi) to still the modifications of the mind (citta-vṛtti-nirodha). Liberation (kaivalya) is the cessation of the guṇa-afflictions and the realization of the pure Self (puruṣa) distinct from prakṛti. The term 'yoga' also denotes the practical discipline of the Gītā (karma-, jñāna-, bhakti-yoga) and contemporary physical and meditation traditions.

title: Abhiṣeka
description: The ritual bathing of a deity or sacred object with water, milk, curd, honey, etc.; its materials, mantras, and occasions vary by tradition and Āgama.

title: Annaprāśana
description: The seventh saṃskāra, the first feeding of solid food, typically in the sixth month; its timing and food items vary by tradition.

title: Antyeṣṭi
description: The final sacrament or funeral rites, whose procedures and underlying eschatology differ across texts, regions, and communities.

title: Ārati
description: The waving of lights before a deity as the culminating offering in worship; its form, number of lamps, and accompanying hymns vary by tradition.

title: Arcana
description: The ritual worship of a deity through sequential offerings (upacāras), typically in temple or home shrine; its sequence and items vary by tradition.

title: Bhajan
description: A devotional song or hymn, often in vernacular languages, sung individually or in groups; its forms, languages, and musical styles are diverse across regions and traditions.

title: Cūḍākaraṇa
description: The eighth saṃskāra, the first haircut (tonsure), typically in the first or third year; its timing and rites vary by text and regional tradition.

title: Dhyāna
description: A contemplative practice term whose methods and aims vary across philosophical and living traditions.

title: Garbhādhāna
description: The first saṃskāra, the rite of conception or impregnation, prescribed in Dharmaśātra for the desire of progeny; its observance varies by text and tradition.

title: Havana
description: Synonym for homa, the fire offering ritual; represented here as a catalogue entry without duplicating the homa record.

title: Homa
description: The fire offering (homa/havana) in which oblations are poured into the sacred fire; its mantras, materials, and purposes vary by Vedic school and occasion.

title: Japa
description: A practice category involving repeated recitation in varied contexts; traditions differ in mantra, method and guidance.

title: Jātakarma
description: The fourth saṃskāra, the birth rite performed immediately after delivery; its mantras and procedures vary across texts and family traditions.

title: Karṇavedha
description: The ninth saṃskāra, the ear-piercing rite; its timing, method, and gender applicability vary across texts and regional customs.

title: Kīrtana
description: A form of devotional call-and-response singing, often accompanied by instruments; its structure, repertoire, and performance contexts vary across traditions and regions.

title: Nāma Saṅkīrtana
description: The congregational chanting of divine names, central to many bhakti traditions; its forms, melodies, and organizational structures vary widely.

title: Nāmakaraṇa
description: The fifth saṃskāra, the naming ceremony typically performed on the eleventh or twelfth day after birth; its timing and customs vary regionally.

title: Niṣkramaṇa
description: The sixth saṃskāra, the first outing of the child, traditionally in the fourth month; its observance varies by text and family custom.

title: Pañca Mahāyajña
description: The five great daily sacrifices—devayajña, ṛṣiyajña, pitṛyajña, bhūtayajña, manusyayajña—prescribed in Dharmaśāstra for householders.

title: Pañcāmṛta
description: The "five nectars" (milk, curd, ghee, honey, sugar) mixed as a ritual offering and later distributed as prasāda; proportions and additional ingredients vary regionally.

title: Prāṇa Pratiṣṭhā
description: The ritual installation of the life-force (prāṇa) into a temple image (mūrti), transforming it into a living embodiment of the deity; its elaborate procedures vary by Āgama tradition.

title: Pravacana
description: A scriptural discourse or sermon, traditionally delivered by a learned teacher; its content, language, and setting vary across traditions and audiences.

title: Pūjā
description: A broad practice category whose forms, meanings and procedures vary by tradition, place and community. This entry defines the category; for specific rites and procedures see the individual practice and ritual records (e.g. archana, arati, sandhyavandana, the saṃskāras, and the temple rituals of a particular Āgama).

title: Puṃsavana
description: The second saṃskāra, performed during pregnancy for the well-being of the fetus; its timing and procedure vary across Dharmaśāstra texts.

title: Samāvartana
description: The eleventh saṃskāra, the completion of Vedic studentship and return home; its observance marks the transition from brahmacarya to gṛhastha.

title: Saṃskāra
description: Saṃskāra (संस्कार) are the subliminal mental impressions formed by action, experience, and conditioned repetition, the psychophysical substrate of saṃsāric continuity in Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain thought. Patañjali's Yoga Sūtras (2.11–18) describe saṃskāras as latent impressions (āśaya) that condition present and future experience; they are the fuel (śakti) of the three kleśas (afflictions) and are exhausted by sustained practice (abhyāsa) and non-attachment (vairāgya). Karmakāṇḍa rites produce saṃskāras of fitness for higher knowledge, while Buddhist Vipassanā counts 84,000 defilements (kammaṭṭhāna) to be dissolved.

title: Sandhyāvandana
description: A daily observance associated with the junctures of the day, whose specific mantras and procedures differ by Vedic school and family tradition.

title: Ṣoḍaśopacāra
description: The "sixteen offerings" (upacāras) in formal deity worship: invocation, seat, water, etc.; the exact list and sequence vary by tradition and Āgama.

title: Śrāddha
description: The ancestral offering rites whose procedures, timing, and eligibility vary across textual prescriptions and regional practices.

title: Sīmantonnayana
description: The third saṃskāra, the parting of the hair rite performed during late pregnancy; its observance varies by text and regional tradition.

title: Svādhyāya
description: The practice of self-study or recitation of one's Vedic branch; a niyama in Yoga philosophy and a daily duty in Dharmaśāstra traditions.

title: Tapas
description: A term for austerity, heat, or disciplined effort whose forms and purposes vary across Vedic, Yoga, and Purāṇic contexts.

title: Tīrtha and pilgrimage
description: A category for pilgrimage and sacred journeys whose meanings and practices vary by place and tradition.

title: Upanayana
description: The initiation ceremony conferring Vedic studentship, whose age, rites, and social applicability differ across textual and community contexts.

title: Vidyārambha
description: The tenth saṃskāra, the commencement of formal education, often coinciding with upanayana or performed separately; its rites vary by tradition.

title: Vivāha
description: The marriage sacrament whose rituals, mantras, and legal frameworks vary across textual prescriptions and regional customary practices.

title: Vrata
description: A category of vows or observances whose forms and meanings vary by region, text and tradition.

title: Yajña
description: A ritual category with different textual, historical and contemporary contexts. The word 'yajña' (sacrifice) can denote (1) the Vedic fire-ritual (e.g. the agṇi-hotra, the soma-yajña, the ṣrauta yajñas), (2) the offering itself (the 'devayana' / 'pindārtha' offerings to the gods, ancestors, and guests), and (3) the broader sense of 'righteous action performed as sacrifice' (karma-yajña) — as elaborated in the Bhagavad Gītā. Specific procedures and vidhānas are given under the individual ritual records referenced by agama, śrauta, and smṛti sources.

title: Āditya Purāṇa
description: The Āditya Purāṇa, one of the eighteen Upapurāṇas, focusing on the worship of Sūrya (Āditya), solar deities, and solar rituals.

title: Agni Purāṇa
description: The Agni Purāṇa, one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas in approximately 383 chapters, transmitted as a discourse of Agni to the sage Vasiṣṭha. Its encyclopedic scope covers cosmology (sarga, pratisarga), geography (dvīpa, varṣa), temple architecture and iconography (pratimā-lakṣaṇa), medicine (Āyurveda), polity (rāja-dharma), Dharmaśāstra topics (saṃskāras, vrata, dāna), and yoga. It preserves the Lakṣmī-kalpa and the Śiva-rātra sections. A key source for traditional Indian knowledge systems. ---

title: Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā
description: The Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā, a major Vaiṣṇava Pāñcarātra text, focusing on the Sudarśana cakra, the Nṛsiṃha mantra, the cakra system, and the esoteric rituals of the Pāñcarātra tradition.

title: Aitareya Āraṇyaka
description: The Aitareya Āraṇyaka, associated with the Ṛgveda, contains the Aitareya Upaniṣad and discusses the inner meaning of ritual.

title: Aitareya Brāhmaṇa
description: The Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, associated with the Śākalya Śākhā of the Ṛgveda, provides ritual prescriptions and theological explanations.

title: Aitareya Upaniṣad
description: An Upaniṣad associated with the Ṛgveda, represented here through an original catalogue description.

title: Ajita Āgama
description: The Ajita Āgama, one of the twenty-eight principal Śaiva Āgamas, covering the four pādas with emphasis on the nature of Śiva as Ajita (unconquered), temple rituals, and the philosophy of Śiva-Śakti.

title: Akṣi Upaniṣad
description: The Akṣi Upaniṣad, associated with the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, focuses on the nature of the eye (akṣi) as a symbol of knowledge and the means to realize the inner self through vidyā.

title: Aṃśumān Āgama
description: The Aṃśumān Āgama, one of the twenty-eight principal Śaiva Āgamas, focusing on the radiant (aṃśumān) aspect of Śiva as the source of all light and knowledge.

title: Aṅka Āgama
description: The Aṅka Āgama, one of the twenty-eight principal Śaiva Āgamas, detailing the distinguishing marks (aṅka) of Śiva's various forms and the iconographic prescriptions for temple images.

title: Āpastamba Dharmasūtra
description: The Āpastamba Dharmasūtra, associated with the Taittirīya Śākhā of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, is one of the earliest Dharma Sūtras prescribing social, legal, and ritual norms.

title: Āraṇyaka texts
description: The "forest texts" bridging Vedic ritual and Upaniṣadic speculation; represented here as a category rather than individual texts.

title: Āruṇi Upaniṣad
description: The Āruṇi Upaniṣad, associated with the Sāmaveda, is a saṃnyāsa Upaniṣad discussing the renunciant's life, the praṇava (oṃ), and the nature of Brahman.

title: Atharvaveda Saṃhitā
description: The Atharvaveda Saṃhitā, the fourth Veda, containing hymns and prose for healing, protection, and domestic rituals, transmitted in Śaunaka and Paippalāda recensions.

title: Atharvaveda
description: A Vedic collection represented as a concise catalogue record. Interpretive and recensional differences require separate sourcing.

title: Auśanasa Purāṇa
description: The Auśanasa Purāṇa, one of the eighteen Upapurāṇas, attributed to the sage Uśanas (Śukra), focusing on dharma, polity, and the worship of Śiva.

title: Avadhūta Upaniṣad
description: The Avadhūta Upaniṣad, a saṃnyāsa Upaniṣad, presents the teachings of Dattātreya on the liberated state (avadhūta) beyond all social and ritual conventions.

title: Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra
description: The Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra, associated with the Taittirīya Śākhā of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, is one of the earliest Dharma Sūtras and includes the Baudhāyana Śrauta and Gṛhya Sūtras.

title: Madhva Bhagavad Gītā Bhāṣya
description: Madhva's Gītā Bhāṣya, presenting the Dvaita interpretation, emphasizing the fivefold difference (pañca-bheda), the hierarchy of souls, and the supremacy of bhakti to Viṣṇu.

title: Nimbārka Bhagavad Gītā Bhāṣya
description: Nimbārka's Gītā Bhāṣya, presenting the Bhedābheda interpretation, reconciling difference and non-difference through the relation of whole and part.

title: Rāmānuja Bhagavad Gītā Bhāṣya
description: Rāmānuja's Gītā Bhāṣya, presenting the Viśiṣṭādvaita interpretation of the Gītā, emphasizing bhakti as the supreme path and the role of prapatti (self-surrender).

title: Śaṅkara Bhagavad Gītā Bhāṣya
description: Śaṅkara's Bhagavad Gītā Bhāṣya, the earliest surviving commentary on the Gītā (c. 8th century), establishing the Advaita interpretation of karma-yoga, jñāna-yoga, and bhakti-yoga as convergent paths to liberation.

title: Śrīdhara Bhagavad Gītā Bhāṣya
description: Śrīdhara's Gītā Bhāṣya (Subodhinī), an influential Advaita commentary known for its clarity and systematic exposition.

title: Vallabha Bhagavad Gītā Bhāṣya
description: Vallabha's Bhagavad Gītā Bhāṣya (Subodhinī), presenting the Śuddhādvaita interpretation, emphasizing puṣṭi (grace) as the means to participate in Kṛṣṇa's līlā.

title: Bhagavad Gītā Chapter 1 — Arjuna Viṣāda Yoga
description: Bhagavad Gītā Chapter 1 (Āropaṇa, 'the setting') presents the Kuru army arrayed, the despair of the Pandavas, and Arjuna's crisis of dharma when he sees the elders and teachers in arms. The 'Oṅkāra' of Arjuna's lament and the Gītā's inaugural 'dharma-kṣetre' set up the conflict between worldly loyalty and righteous duty that the Gītā's discourse resolves through the teaching of yoga.

title: Bhagavad Gītā Chapter 10 — Vibhūti Yoga
description: Gītā Chapter 10 (Vibhūti-yoga, 'the manifestation') presents the 'glories' (vibhūti) of the Supreme, enumerating the divine powers (īśvara-bala) and the supreme Person's manifestations as kings, as the Vedas, and as the foremost of the devotees. It balances the transcendence (para) and the immanence (aparā) and affirms that the wise see the same (ekatva) in all beings.

title: Bhagavad Gītā Chapter 11 — Viśvarūpa Darśana Yoga
description: Gītā Chapter 11 (Vilāpa-yoga, 'the universal form') records Arjuna's petition to see the supreme Person's cosmic form (viśvarūpa), which Kṛṣṇa grants. The vision is cosmic (the whole of time and space) and terrifying (kālī), revealing the universal (sarvataḥ pāṇi) yet intimate presence of the divine. Arjuna's grief and surrender (praṇāma) mark the culmination of his bhakti and the 'crowning' (śiras) of the Gītā's teaching.

title: Bhagavad Gītā Chapter 12 — Bhakti Yoga
description: Gītā Chapter 12 (Bhakti-yoga, 'the yoga of devotion') is prefaced by Arjuna's question (which of the 'higher' path — of the formless [nirguṇa] or the 'with-form' [saguṇa]). Kṛṣṇa answers that the path of devotion (bhakti) is easier for the embodied, and describes the 'equal-minded' (sama-caraṇa) devotee who sees the self (ātman) and the deity (īśvara) as one and serves all beings as manifestations of the supreme.

title: Bhagavad Gītā Chapter 13 — Kṣetra Kṣetrajña Vibhāga Yoga
description: Gītā Chapter 13 (Kṣetra-kṣetrātmārāmāya, 'the field and the knower of the field') presents the doctrine of the field (kṣetra, the body-mind) and the knower (kṣetrajña, the self) as the subject of discriminative knowledge (jñāna). It identifies the supreme knowledge (parama-jñāna) with the knowledge of the field-kṣetraṅkṣaṇa (the self's distinction from prakṛti) and teaches that such knowledge brings the seeker to the supreme (para).

title: Bhagavad Gītā Chapter 14 — Guṇa Traya Vibhāga Yoga
description: Gītā Chapter 14 (Guṇatraya-vibhāgayoga) explains the three Guṇas (sattva, rajas, tamas) as the conditioning of the embodied self and the basis of the 'wheel of birth' (samsāra). It teaches the 'transcendence' (viśeṣaṇa) beyond the guṇas as the mark of the great (mahātmā) and the 'liberated' (mokṣa) who has gone beyond the 'three-fold' guṇa-bondage.

title: Bhagavad Gītā Chapter 15 — Puruṣottama Yoga
description: Gītā Chapter 15 (Puruṣottama-yoga, 'the supreme person') introduces the 'tree of the world' (aśvattha) whose roots are above and branches below — the symbol of the embodied (dehī) versus the supreme (parama) person. It presents the two 'fruits' of the wise (jñāna) and the two birds (sādhana) and concludes with the teaching that the supreme Person (puruṣottama) alone is the goal beyond the field of action.

title: Bhagavad Gītā Chapter 16 — Daivāsura Sampad Vibhāga Yoga
description: Gītā Chapter 16 (Daivāsura-yoga, 'divine and demonic') contrasts the divine (daivī) qualities (fear of God, non-violence, truthfulness, self-control) with the demonic (āsurī) (hypocrisy, arrogance, violence, anger). It teaches that the divine-natured inherit the supreme (para) while the demoniac are doomed to repeated birth; it is the explicit moral framework of the Gītā's teaching.

title: Bhagavad Gītā Chapter 17 — Śraddhā Traya Vibhāga Yoga
description: Gītā Chapter 17 (Śraddhā-vibhāgayoga, 'the threefold faith') presents the threefold classification of things — faith (śraddhā), the food (āhāra), the sacrifice (yajña), the austerity (tapas), the speech (vāk), and the deed (karmā) — as the expression of the seeker's disposition (guṇa). It teaches that faith is the root (mūla) of the seeker and that the threefold nature of the seeker determines the threefold path (karma, jñāna, bhakti).

title: Bhagavad Gītā Chapter 18 — Mokṣa Saṃnyāsa Yoga
description: Gītā Chapter 18 (Mokṣa-yoga, 'the yoga of liberation') concludes with the threefold classification of knowledge (jñāna), the doer (karta), and 'renunciation' (tyāga) — 'knowledge-knowledge' (para), 'action-action' (phala), and renunciation (niṣkāma). It summarizes the teaching (the four Puruṣārthas and the three yogas) and Arjuna's final resolution (kṣipra) to fight as the instrument (ṇāyakā) of the divine.

title: Bhagavad Gītā Chapter 2 — Sāṅkhya Yoga
description: Gītā Chapter 2 (Sāṅkhya Yoga) opens Kṛṣṇa's teaching with the impermanence of the body and the immortality of the ātman (the body is discarded like cast-off garments). It distinguishes the field (kṣetra) and the knower of the field, defines yoga as skill in action, and contrasts the transient (dehī) with the eternal (nāśa-bandhu). It is the canonical locus of the doctrines of karma-yoga, jñāna-yoga, and the teaching that mokṣa comes only through knowledge (jñāna) of the self's identity with Brahman.

title: Bhagavad Gītā Chapter 3 — Karma Yoga
description: Gītā Chapter 3 (Karma-yoga) establishes action (karma) as inescapable for embodied beings and teaches the yoga of selfless action (niṣkāma karma). It introduces the doctrine of the 'wheel' (cakara) of action that cannot be escaped by the seeker, the teaching that performance must be dedicated to the divine (īśvarārpaṇa), and the example of the sage who acts without attachment (yukta-vairāgya).

title: Bhagavad Gītā Chapter 4 — Jñāna Karma Saṃnyāsa Yoga
description: Gītā Chapter 4 (Jñāna-karma-saṅgama) presents the simultaneous path of knowledge and action, the doctrine of the 'divine birth' (daśa-guṇa) of the avatar, and Kṛṣṇa's revelation that he has taught the imperishable yoga to the sun (Vaivasvata) and through the ages to the seers. It is the source of the celebrated line 'sarva-dharmān parityajya māṁ ekam śaraṇaṁ vraja' (abandon all dharmas and take refuge in me alone).

title: Bhagavad Gītā Chapter 5 — Karma Saṃnyāsa Yoga
description: Gītā Chapter 5 (Karma-sannyāsa-yoga) contrasts the path of renunciation (karma-sannyāsa) with the path of action (karma-yoga) and resolves them in the yoga of the self (ātma-yoga). It presents the doctrine of 'the fruit' (phala) and 'the fruitless' (aphala) actions, the two birds (sakhya) on the branch of the world-tree, and the equality (sama) of mind toward pleasure-pain, heat-cold, and friend-foe as the mark of the liberated (jīvanmukta).

title: Bhagavad Gītā Chapter 6 — Dhyāna Yoga
description: Gītā Chapter 6 (Dhyāna-yoga / Ātma-saṅgraha) teaches the practical discipline (abhyāsa-vairāgya) of meditation (dhyāna), the six modifications (vṛtti) of the mind, and the attainment (prāpti) of samādhi and the peace (śānti) that transcends ordinary mind. It warns against the self-centered (ātma) practice without mastery and commends the sthira-sukham (steady-happiness) of the sage who rests in the absolute.

title: Bhagavad Gītā Chapter 7 — Jñāna Vijñāna Yoga
description: Gītā Chapter 7 (Jñāna-vijñāna-yoga) declares Kṛṣṇa as the supreme (para) of the knowledge and the secret of his being (guhyatama), and teaches the four kinds of seekers (the distressed, the desirous, the seeker of knowledge, and the learned). It is the doctrinal basis of the Kṛṣṇa-centric bhakti of the Gauḍīya and presents the 'knowledge-that-is-secret-of-the-self' (jñāna) as the key to the whole teaching.

title: Bhagavad Gītā Chapter 8 — Akṣara Brahma Yoga
description: Gītā Chapter 8 (Atharva-vākya-yoga, 'the last word') returns to the question of what is the imperishable (akṣara) and what is the supreme (para). It introduces the 'word/verse' (śabda/ākṣara) as the means, presents the death-bed teaching (para-kāla) and the various paths to the supreme goal (including the remembering of the name [nāma-smṛti] and the yoga of the breath).

title: Bhagavad Gītā Chapter 9 — Rāja Vidyā Rāja Guhya Yoga
description: Gītā Chapter 9 (Rāja-yoga, 'the king of knowledge') is the 'jewel of all teachings,' declaring the supreme Person (parama-puruṣa) Kṛṣṇa and the path of devotion (bhakti) that is open to all (the outcaste, the woman, the devotee alike). It is the locus of the 'equal-eyed' (sama-darśi) vision and the teaching that the supreme pervades all beings and yet is distinct from them (anumantavyāḥ).

title: Bhagavad Gita
description: The Bhagavad Gītā (c. 2nd c. BCE–2nd c. CE, 700 verses) is the philosophical core of the Mahābhārata (Bhīṣma Parva, chap. 23–40) and the dialogue between Kṛṣṇa and the reluctant Arjuna on the field of Kurukṣetra. It synthesizes the three yogas — karma (selfless action), jñāna (knowledge), bhakti (devotion) — and affirms the four Puruṣārthas. Its doctrines (līlā, mokṣa, the gunas, the supreme person of the Gītā, nis-kāma karma) shaped the Vedānta, the bhakti movement, and modern Indian political and religious thought (Gandhi, Tilak, Aurobindo). It is the most translated and most commented Hindu text.

title: Bhāgavata Purāṇa
description: The Bhāgavata Purāṇa (Śrīmad Bhāgavatam), one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas in twelve skandhas (books) and ~18,000 verses. Composed as a dialogue between Śuka and King Parīkṣit on the banks of the Gaṅgā. Skandha 1-2: creation, cosmology, and the avatāras; Skandha 3-4: Kapila's Sāṅkhya, Dhruva, Prahlāda; Skandha 5: Bharata, Ṛṣabha, cosmic geography; Skandha 6: Ajāmila, Vaivasvata, Nṛsiṃha; Skandha 7: Prahlāda, Nṛsiṃha; Skandha 8: Vāmana, churning of the ocean; Skandha 9: genealogies; Skandha 10: Kṛṣṇa's līlā (Vṛndāvana, Mathurā, Dvārakā); Skandha 11: Uddhava-gītā, Yadu dynasty; Skandha 12: future, Kali age, Māhātmya. Central to Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism and bhakti traditions across India. ---

title: Bhārgava Purāṇa
description: The Bhārgava Purāṇa, one of the eighteen Upapurāṇas, attributed to the sage Bhṛgu, focusing on dharma, prāyaścitta, and the worship of Viṣṇu.

title: Bhaviṣya Purāṇa
description: The Bhaviṣya Purāṇa, one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas in four parts (Brāhma, Madhyama, Pratisarga, Uttara) and ~28,000 verses, narrated by Sūta to the sages at Naimiṣāraṇya. Known for its "future" (bhaviṣya) orientation — prophecies, royal genealogies of future dynasties (Maurya, Gupta, Harsha, medieval Indian rulers, and even British period references), the Sūrya-vaṃśa and Candra-vaṃśa lineages, the Sāyaṇācārya's solar worship, the Kṛṣṇa-līlā, the Tulasī-māhātmya, the Rāma-nāma-māhātmya, the Kāśī-māhātmya, the Gayā-śrāddha, and numerous vrata-kathās. The only Purāṇa with extensive historical/prophetic content on post-Vedic Indian dynasties. Controversial for its late interpolations; the Pratisargaparvan is considered a later addition. ---

title: Bimbāmbikā Āgama
description: The Bimbāmbikā Āgama, one of the twenty-eight principal Śaiva Āgamas, associated with the Goddess Bimbāmbikā (a form of Śakti) and the Śaiva-Śākta synthesis in temple worship.

title: Brahma Purāṇa
description: The Brahma Purāṇa, one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas in ~10,000 verses, traditionally ascribed to Brahmā and narrated to the sages at Naimiṣāraṇya. Covers creation (sarga), the solar and lunar dynasties, the geography of Bhārata-varṣa, the seven dvīpas, the glory of the Godāvarī and other rivers, the Śiva and Viṣṇu kṣetras (Ekāmra, Purī, Koṇārka, Kāśī), the Purī Jagannātha temple, the Ratha-yātrā, and the Saura and Gāṇapatya traditions. Contains the Gautamī-māhātmya (Godāvarī pilgrimage) and the Koṇārka-māhātmya. Bridges Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, and Saura traditions; especially important for Odisha and Andhra temple mythology. ---

title: Brahma Sūtra Adhyāya 1 — Samanvaya
description: The first adhyāya (chapter) of the Brahma Sūtra (Samanvaya), consisting of four pādas and 134 sūtras, harmonizing the diverse Upaniṣadic statements to establish that Brahman is the sole cause of the universe.

title: Brahma Sūtra Adhyāya 2 — Avirodha
description: The second adhyāya of the Brahma Sūtra (Avirodha), consisting of four pādas and 157 sūtras, refuting objections from other schools (Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Vaiśeṣika, Buddhist, Jain) and showing the consistency of the Vedānta doctrine.

title: Brahma Sūtra Adhyāya 3 — Sādhana
description: The third adhyāya of the Brahma Sūtra (Sādhana), consisting of four pādas and 186 sūtras, discussing the means (sādhana) to realize Brahman, including meditation (upāsanā), ethics, and the path of knowledge.

title: Brahma Sūtra Adhyāya 4 — Phala
description: The fourth adhyāya of the Brahma Sūtra (Phala), consisting of four pādas and 113 sūtras, describing the fruit (phala) of knowledge — liberation (mokṣa), the state of the liberated, and the fate of the knower of Brahman.

title: Madhva Brahma Sūtra Bhāṣya
description: Madhva's Brahma Sūtra Bhāṣya, the Dvaita commentary on the Brahma Sūtra, establishing the fivefold eternal difference (pañca-bheda) and Viṣṇu as the supreme independent reality.

title: Nimbārka Vedānta Pārijāta Saurabha
description: Nimbārka's Vedānta Pārijāta Saurabha, the Bhedābheda commentary on the Brahma Sūtra, establishing difference-and-non-difference with Kṛṣṇa as the supreme reality.

title: Prakāśātman Brahma Sūtra Bhāṣya
description: Prakāśātman's Brahma Sūtra Bhāṣya (Pancapadika), a detailed Advaita commentary elaborating on the first five sūtras of the Brahma Sūtra.

title: Rāmānuja Śrī Bhāṣya on Brahma Sūtra
description: Rāmānuja's Śrī Bhāṣya, the principal Viśiṣṭādvaita commentary on the Brahma Sūtra, establishing qualified non-duality with Viṣṇu as the supreme Brahman qualified by conscious souls and matter.

title: Śaṅkara Brahma Sūtra Bhāṣya
description: Śaṅkara's Brahma Sūtra Bhāṣya, the earliest surviving and most influential commentary on the Brahma Sūtra, establishing the Advaita (non-dual) interpretation.

title: Sureśvara Brahma Sūtra Bhāṣya
description: Sureśvara's Brahma Sūtra Bhāṣya (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Bhāṣya Vārtika), the direct disciple of Śaṅkara, providing a detailed Vārtika on Śaṅkara's Brahma Sūtra Bhāṣya.

title: Vācaspati Miśra Brahma Sūtra Bhāṣya
description: Vācaspati Miśra's Brahma Sūtra Bhāṣya (Bhāmatī), a sub-commentary on Śaṅkara's Brahma Sūtra Bhāṣya, establishing the Bhāmatī school of Advaita and its theory of avidyā.

title: Vallabha Anubhāṣya
description: Vallabha's Anubhāṣya, the Śuddhādvaita commentary on the Brahma Sūtra, establishing pure non-duality with Kṛṣṇa as the supreme Brahman and the path of grace (puṣṭi-mārga).

title: Brahma Sūtra
description: The Brahma Sūtra (Vedānta Sūtra) of Bādarāyaṇa, the foundational text of Vedānta darśana, in four adhyāyas and 555 sūtras.

title: Brahma Upaniṣad
description: The Brahma Upaniṣad, associated with the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, focuses on the nature of Brahman, the self, and the means to liberation through knowledge and meditation.

title: Brahmayāmala Tantra
description: The Brahmayāmala Tantra, a major Śākta Tantra in 21 chapters, focusing on the worship of the Goddess as Brahmayāmala, the cakra system, and the Kaula initiation.

title: Brāhmaṇa texts
description: The ritual commentaries attached to the Vedic Saṃhitās, explaining sacrificial procedures and their symbolic meanings; represented here as a category rather than individual texts.

title: Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa
description: The Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas in four parts (prakriyā, anuṣaṅga, upodghāta, upasaṃhāra) and ~12,000 verses. Details the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), creation cycles, geography of the seven dvīpas, the Aṣṭādaśa-śakti-pīṭhas (eighteen Goddess shrines), and the Lalitopākhyāna (narrative of Lalitā Tripurasundarī) in the Uttarārdha. Contains the Āditya-hṛdaya, the Navagraha-stotras, and detailed pilgrimage (tīrtha) sections for Kāñcī, Śrīśaila, and other Śākta sites. Closely related to the Vāyu Purāṇa; together they preserve the Āditya and Śaiva-Śākta cosmologies. Key for Śākta tradition and South Indian temple mythology. ---

title: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad
description: The longest Upaniṣad, associated with the Śukla Yajurveda, represented here through an original catalogue description.

title: Bṛhaspati Smṛti
description: The Bṛhaspati Smṛti, a Dharmaśāstra text attributed to Bṛhaspati, focusing on vyavahāra (legal procedure), courts, evidence, and civil law.

title: Chandaḥsūtra
description: The Chandaḥsūtra of Piṅgala is the foundational text of the Vedāṅga of metre (chandas), presenting the combinatorial analysis of Vedic and classical metres.

title: Chāndogya Brāhmaṇa
description: The Chāndogya Brāhmaṇa (the first part of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad's textual complex), associated with the Kauthuma Śākhā of the Sāmaveda, contains the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.

title: Chāndogya Upaniṣad
description: One of the longest Upaniṣads, associated with the Sāmaveda, represented here through an original catalogue description.

title: Cintya Āgama
description: The Cintya Āgama, one of the twenty-eight principal Śaiva Āgamas, focusing on the jñāna pāda and the contemplative (cintya) knowledge of Śiva as the supreme consciousness.

title: Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa
description: The Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa (Śrī Devī Bhāgavatam), a major Śākta Mahāpurāṇa in 12 skandhas and ~18,000 verses, modeled on the Bhāgavata Purāṇa's structure but centered on the Goddess. Skandha 1: creation, the Goddess as śakti; Skandha 2-3: the Devī's forms, the battle with Mahiṣāsura; Skandha 4: the Devī-gītā (the Goddess's teaching on jñāna, yoga, bhakti); Skandha 5: the Śākta cosmology, the Śrī-cakra, the nine nityās; Skandha 6: the Kālī-krama, the ten Mahāvidyās; Skandha 7: the Navarātrī vrata, the Caṇḍī-pāṭha procedure; Skandha 8-9: the glories of Śākta pīṭhas (Kāmākhyā, Kālikā, Tārāpīṭha); Skandha 10-11: the Rāma and Kṛṣṇa narratives retold from the Śākta perspective; Skandha 12: liberation through Devī-bhakti. The primary text for the Devī-gītā and Śākta theology, influential in Bengal and Assam.

title: Dīpta Āgama
description: The Dīpta Āgama, one of the twenty-eight principal Śaiva Āgamas, known for its treatment of the caryā pāda (conduct) and the radiant (dīpta) manifestation of Śiva in the world.

title: Dvijaja Āgama
description: The Dvijaja Āgama, one of the twenty-eight principal Śaiva Āgamas, associated with the twice-born (dvija) tradition of Śaiva initiation and the transmission of mantras through the guru-śiṣya lineage.

title: Garbha Upaniṣad
description: The Garbha Upaniṣad, associated with the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, describes the development of the embryo, the constitution of the body, and the relationship between the physical body and the subtle self.

title: Garga Purāṇa
description: The Garga Purāṇa, one of the eighteen Upapurāṇas, attributed to the sage Garga, focusing on astrology (jyotiṣa), omens, and the worship of Kṛṣṇa.

title: Garuḍa Purāṇa
description: The Garuḍa Purāṇa, one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas in ~19,000 verses, narrated by Garuḍa to Kaśyapa (or Viṣṇu to Garuḍa). Two main parts: Pūrvakhanda (Ācāra-kāṇḍa, Dharma-kāṇḍa, Preta-kāṇḍa) and Uttarakhanda (Brahma-kāṇḍa). Covers Viṣṇu worship, saṃskāras, vrata, dāna, temple construction, iconography, gemology (ratna-śāstra), astrology, medicine (Āyurveda), the afterlife journey (pretakalpā), the realms of Yama, funeral rites (antyeṣṭi), śrāddha, and the path to liberation through Viṣṇu-bhakti. Authoritative for death rituals and śrāddha procedures across Hindu traditions. ---

title: Gautama Dharmasūtra
description: The Gautama Dharmasūtra, associated with the Sāmaveda, is an early Dharma Sūtra presenting legal, social, and ritual norms.

title: Gopatha Brāhmaṇa
description: The Gopatha Brāhmaṇa, the only Brāhmaṇa of the Atharvaveda (associated with the Śaunaka and Paippalāda Śākhās), provides ritual instructions and explanations specific to Atharvan practice.

title: Gṛhya Sūtra
description: The Gṛhya Sūtras, the Vedāṅga texts of domestic rites (saṃskāras): marriage (vivāha), conception (garbhādhāna), birth (jātakarma), naming (nāmakaraṇa), first feeding (annaprāśana), tonsure (cūḍākaraṇa), initiation (upanayana), marriage, and funeral (antyeṣṭi).

title: Haṃsa Upaniṣad
description: The Haṃsa Upaniṣad, associated with the Śukla Yajurveda, teaches the Haṃsa-vidyā (the knowledge of the inner swan/breath) and the identity of the individual self with the supreme.

title: Harivaṃśa
description: The Harivaṃśa (Lineage of Hari), an appendix (khila) to the Mahābhārata in three books, detailing the lineage of Kṛṣṇa, his childhood in Vraja, and the history of the Yādava dynasty.

title: Īśā Upaniṣad
description: A short Upaniṣadic text represented here through an original catalogue description, without reproducing a translation.

title: Jabāla Upaniṣad
description: The Jabāla Upaniṣad (Jabala Upanishad), associated with the Ṛgveda, discusses prāṇa, the nature of the self, and the path to liberation.

title: Jaiminīya Āraṇyaka
description: The Jaiminīya Āraṇyaka, associated with the Jaiminīya Śākhā of the Sāmaveda, contains the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Bṛhadāraṇyaka and related forest texts.

title: Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa
description: The Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa (also Talavakāra Brāhmaṇa), associated with the Jaiminīya/Talavakāra Śākhā of the Sāmaveda, contains ritual prescriptions and theological explanations.

title: Jayākhya Saṃhitā
description: The Jayākhya Saṃhitā, a major Vaiṣṇava Pāñcarātra text in 33 chapters, expounding the five forms of Viṣṇu (para, vyūha, vibhava, antaryāmin, arcā), the fivefold worship (pañcakāla), and the philosophy of Viṣṇu as supreme.

title: Jyotiṣa Vedāṅga
description: The Jyotiṣa Vedāṅga (Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa) attributed to Lagadha is the foundational text of the Vedāṅga of astronomy and calendrical science, used for determining ritual times.

title: Kaivalya Upaniṣad
description: The Kaivalya Upaniṣad, associated with the Atharvaveda, is a Śaiva-oriented Upaniṣad describing the attainment of kaivalya (liberation) through devotion to Śiva and knowledge of the ātman.

title: Kālikā Purāṇa
description: The Kālikā Purāṇa, one of the eighteen Upapurāṇas, a Śākta text focusing on the worship of Kālī, the ten Mahāvidyās, and the ritual practices of Śākta traditions in Kamarupa (Assam).

title: Kāmika Āgama
description: The Kāmika Āgama, one of the twenty-eight principal Śaiva Āgamas, covering all four pādas (jñāna, yoga, kriyā, caryā) with detailed ritual instructions for temple construction, daily worship, and festivals.

title: Kapila Purāṇa
description: The Kapila Purāṇa, one of the eighteen Upapurāṇas, attributed to the sage Kapila, focusing on Sāṅkhya philosophy, the worship of Viṣṇu, and the glory of the Gangā.

title: Karaṇa Āgama
description: The Karaṇa Āgama, one of the twenty-eight principal Śaiva Āgamas, detailing the kriyā pāda with emphasis on temple rituals, the consecration of liṅgas, and the daily worship sequence (nitya-pūjā).

title: Kaṭha Āraṇyaka
description: The Kaṭha Āraṇyaka, associated with the Kaṭha Śākhā of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, contains the Kaṭha Upaniṣad and related ritual and philosophical material.

title: Kaṭha Upaniṣad
description: An Upaniṣad structured as a dialogue between Naciketas and Yama, represented here through an original catalogue description without reproducing translations.

title: Kātyāyana Smṛti
description: The Kātyāyana Smṛti, a Dharmaśāstra text attributed to Kātyāyana, focusing on vyavahāra, women's property rights (strīdhana), and inheritance law.

title: Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa
description: The Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, associated with the Bāṣkala Śākhā of the Ṛgveda, contains ritual prescriptions and theological explanations.

title: Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad
description: The Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad (also Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa Upaniṣad), associated with the Ṛgveda, discusses prāṇa, the nature of the self, and the path to liberation.

title: Kena Upaniṣad
description: A short Upaniṣadic text focused on the nature of Brahman and the limits of empirical knowledge, represented here through an original catalogue description.

title: Kiraṇa Āgama
description: The Kiraṇa Āgama, one of the twenty-eight principal Śaiva Āgamas, known for its detailed treatment of dīkṣā (initiation), the nature of the soul (paśu), and the removal of mala.

title: Kulārṇava Tantra
description: The Kulārṇava Tantra, a major Śākta Tantra in 17 chapters, expounding the Kaula tradition, the worship of Kuleśvarī, the cakra system, and the guru-śiṣya relationship.

title: Kūrma Purāṇa
description: The Kūrma Purāṇa, one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas in two parts (Pūrvabhāga and Uttarabhāga) and ~17,000 verses, narrated by Kūrma (Viṣṇu's tortoise avatar) to the sages at Naimiṣāraṇya. Pūrvabhāga: creation, the four puruṣārthas (dharma, artha, kāma, mokṣa), the glory of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-hṛdaya, the unity of Śiva and Viṣṇu, the ṛṣi genealogies; Uttarabhāga: the Īśvara-gītā (Śiva's teaching on yoga and jñāna), the Vyāsa-gītā, the Śiva-gītā, pilgrimage to Kāśī, Prayāga, Gayā, and the Śiva kṣetras. A synthesis text emphasizing Śiva-Viṣṇu non-difference (abheda) and the yoga of knowledge and devotion. ---

title: Lakulīśa Pāśupata Sūtra
description: The Lakulīśa Pāśupata Sūtra, the foundational text of the Pāśupata Śaiva tradition founded by Lakulīśa, outlining the five categories (kārana, kārya, yoga, vidhi, duḥkhānta) and the path of the Pāśupata ascetic.

title: Lalitā Āgama
description: The Lalitā Āgama, one of the twenty-eight principal Śaiva Āgamas, associated with the playful (lalita) aspect of Śiva-Śakti union, integrating Śaiva and Śākta ritual streams in the worship of the Divine Couple.

title: Liṅga Purāṇa
description: The Liṅga Purāṇa, one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas in ~11,000 verses and two parts (Pūrvabhāga and Uttarabhāga). Pūrvabhāga: the origin of the liṅga (liṅgodbhava), the glory of the liṅga, the twenty-eight Śaiva Āgamas, the five faces of Śiva (Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, Īśāna), the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti), the twelve jyotirliṅgas; Uttarabhāga: the Liṅga-gītā (Śiva's teaching to the sages), the story of Dhruva, the Puṣkara-māhātmya, the glory of Kāśī, the Śiva-rātra vrata, the rites of liṅga-pratiṣṭhā and daily worship (nitya-pūjā). The definitive textual authority for liṅga worship in Śaiva temple tradition. ---

title: Mahābhārata Ādi Parva
description: The first book (Ādi Parva) of the Mahābhārata, containing the origins of the Kuru dynasty, the birth of the Pāṇḍavas and Kauravas, the game of dice, and the exile of the Pāṇḍavas.

title: Mahābhārata Anuśāsana Parva
description: The thirteenth book (Anuśāsana Parva) of the Mahābhārata, continuing Bhīṣma's teachings on dharma, varṇa, āśrama, and the glory of Viṣṇu.

title: Mahābhārata Āśramavāsika Parva
description: The fourteenth book (Āśramavāsika Parva) of the Mahābhārata, describing the Pāṇḍavas' retirement to the forest, Dhṛtarāṣṭra's death, and the end of the Kuru elders.

title: Mahābhārata Bhīṣma Parva
description: The sixth book (Bhīṣma Parva) of the Mahābhārata, containing the first ten days of the Kurukṣetra war under Bhīṣma's command, including the Bhagavad Gītā.

title: Mahābhārata Droṇa Parva
description: The seventh book (Droṇa Parva) of the Mahābhārata, describing the five days of war under Droṇa's command, including the deaths of Abhimanyu and Droṇa.

title: Mahābhārata Karṇa Parva
description: The eighth book (Karṇa Parva) of the Mahābhārata, describing the two days of war under Karṇa's command and his final duel with Arjuna.

title: Mahābhārata Mahāprasthānika Parva
description: The sixteenth book (Mahāprasthānika Parva) of the Mahābhārata, describing the Pāṇḍavas' great journey (mahāprasthāna) toward the Himalayas and their successive falls.

title: Mahābhārata Mausala Parva
description: The fifteenth book (Mausala Parva) of the Mahābhārata, describing the destruction of the Yādava clan through mutual slaughter (mausala) and Kṛṣṇa's departure.

title: Mahābhārata Sabhā Parva
